articles.title: US Open: Elena Rybakina becomes new women's No. 1 with win over Qinwen Zheng in quarterfinal
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina is a step closer to winning her first-ever US Open title.
articles.body:
There was a lot at stake for Elena Rybakina during her quarterfinal match against Qinwen Zheng on Wednesday. With a victory, Rybakina would not only move a step closer to winning her first US Open, she would also assume the title of the No. 1-ranked women's player in the sport.

Well, move over Aryna Sabalenka, because you've been dethroned. Rybakina advanced Wednesday, beating Zheng in three sets (3-6, 6-1, 6-4) to keep her US Open title hopes alive and become the top-ranked women's player in the world.

Sabalenka had previously held the No. 1 rank for the past 99 weeks. But some earlier-than-expected exits, combined with improved play from Rybakina, put that position in limbo heading into Wednesday. All Rybakina needed was a win over Zheng to take the top spot. It was a hard-fought match, but Rybakina did it.

It marks the first time in her career Rybakina has been ranked No. 1.

It also marks the furthest Rybakina has ever advanced at the US Open. Her previous high came last year, when she reached the fourth round of the event before falling.

Typically, the US Open has proven to be Rybakina's most difficult Grand Slam. Entering play Wednesday, she had won just 57 percent of her matches at the event.

The win not only solidifies Rybakina's status as the top woman in the sport right now but sets her up to potentially capture her third Grand Slam win. Rybakina has already won Wimbledon and the Australian Open. A win at the US Open would leave the French Open as the only Grand Slam she's yet to conquer.

Getting there won't be easy. After narrowly defeating Zheng on Wednesday, Rybakina is guaranteed to take on some of the highest ranked women the rest of the way, as many of the favorites on the women's side advanced to the quarterfinals.

As her new No. 1 ranking suggests, Rybakina should be up for any challenge at this point … even if she manages to trail early.

Qinwen Zheng outlasts Elena Rybakina in first set

That's exactly what happened Wednesday, as Rybakina and Zheng got off to an exciting start, trading the first seven games in the first set. In Game 8, Zheng finally broke Rybakina to take a 5-3 lead. Rybakina nearly did the same in the ninth game, taking three of the first four points in the game. But Zheng battled back, with the game eventually getting the deuce.

From there, Rybakina and Zheng reached an advantage a combined seven times before Zheng was finally able to close out the game. In doing so, she took the first set 6-3.

Both players appeared to be trying hard for aces in the first set, as neither managed a first serve percentage above 50. Zheng was more successful on that front, notching four aces against Rybakina's one in the set.

Elena Rybakina hits her stride in second set

It was a much different story in the second set. Rybakina got a better handle on her serve, while Zheng often failed to put her first attempt in play. During the set, Rybakina was successful on 58 percent of her first-serve attempts. Zheng clocked in at 38 percent. While it wasn't a flawless game from Rybakina — who had more unforced errors and two double faults — it didn't look that way on paper.

Rybakina cruised to a 6-1 win in the second set, breaking Zheng twice to pick up the victory and send the match to a third set.

After a tense final set, Rybakina pulls out the win

Both players locked in during the final set. With both consistently getting their first-serve attempts in, Rybakina and Zheng traded the first eight games in the set.

It wasn't until the ninth game that Rybakina finally broke Zheng. That set up a 10th game in which Rybakina would serve with the match potentially on the line.

She got the job done, finally dispatching Zheng — who has proven to be a thorn in the side of many higher-ranked opponents at the event — and moving to the semifinals.

Even with the loss, Zheng proved she's nearly back to form after battling injuries early in 2026. After first-round exits at both the French Open and Wimbledon, Zheng showed the form that allowed her to take gold at the 2024 Olympics. If she can retain that, Zheng should shoot back up the rankings after injuries resulted in her fall.

For Rybakina, she can keep her eyes on the prize. There's no better way to follow up her coronation than to go out and win a Grand Slam. If she can do that, she'll leave no doubt she deserves to be No. 1.

articles.title: US Open: Top-seeded quartet set for women's semi-final showdown with Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff in action
articles.summary: Hat-trick hunting Aryna Sabalenka takes on Jessica Pegula with new world No 1 Elena Rybakina facing home favourite Coco Gauff in the semi-finals; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
For the first time since Wimbledon in ​2009, all four top seeds at a Grand Slam have reached the semi-finals, with Sabalenka, Rybakina and Gauff all former major champions and third seed Pegula seeking a maiden Grand Slam title.

Sabalenka has reached the semi-finals here for a sixth consecutive year and is now two wins away from becoming the first woman ‌since Serena Williams from 2012 to 2014 to win three straight titles in New York.

The top seed had not dropped a set before surviving her toughest test of the tournament ​on Tuesday, edging Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova .

The Belarusian will face a familiar opponent in third seed Pegula, with their rivalry returning to Flushing Meadows for a third straight year after Sabalenka denied the American the title in 2024 and then beat her ​again in last year's semi-finals.

Sabalenka leads their head-to-head 9-4 but Pegula has won two of their last three ⁠encounters, including a victory in the Berlin Open semi-finals earlier this year ⁠in which she took the deciding set 6-0.

"I think it's fun to look at the rivalry we've had. She's got to me here the last couple of years," Pegula said.

"I have been able to beat ‌her a few times, maybe on a smaller stage, so I think that's going to be kind of a hurdle for me to get over."

Sabalenka will head into the semi-final after surrendering top spot in the world rankings, which Rybakina secured with her quarter-final victory over Olympic champion Qinwen Zheng.

The Australian Open winner will become the 30th woman to top the WTA rankings and the first from Kazakhstan to reach world No 1 when the new rankings are released after the ⁠tournament.

Sabalenka, who had held the top spot since October 2024, said she would gladly trade it for ​another US Open title.

"I'll be more than happy," she said. "Yes, three-peat. Sounds great."

New world No 1 up against the fan-favourite

Rybakina's reward for reaching the semi-finals for the first time in New York is a meeting with fan-favourite ​Gauff, who produced a stunning comeback to beat fifth seed and fellow French Open winner Mirra Andreeva .

The 2023 ⁠US Open champion was on the brink of defeat in the second set before saving two match points and turning the match around.

Gauff's victory put her into the semi-finals at a second straight Slam after her run to the last four at Wimbledon, and she will have the home crowd behind ⁠her as she bids to clinch a second US Open title.

"Elena is playing some great tennis," said Gauff. "Congrats to her for being the new world No 1 or will be the new World No 1. I think that's incredible.

"We played each other in Toronto. That didn't go my way, so I think I just have to learn from that match.

"I know I'm going to have some aces hit on me and some winners hit on me, but I'm going to keep fighting and give it my all."

A third Slam title or revenge for Gauff?

Rybakina will bid ​for a third Grand Slam title, while Gauff will have revenge on her mind after the Kazakh beat her in ​three sets in last month's Canadian Open semi-finals.

On playing Gauff, Rybakina said: "I will expect that a lot of people are going to support her.

"I just need to stay aggressive. I think from where I was coming to this tournament, being injured and not practicing, I think we came pretty far. Now we just last push and important to still enjoy. Hopefully it's going to go my way."

The pair are tied 1-1 in their previous meetings and will face off for a place in Saturday's final.

articles.title: US Open Tennis 2026 Top Storylines to Watch in Men's Semifinals Bracket
articles.summary: No American man has won a Grand Slam since Andy Roddick won the 2003 US Open.
articles.body:
No American man has won a Grand Slam since Andy Roddick won the 2003 US Open.

However, an American man will compete in a major final for just the second time in the past 15 years.

On Friday, Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe will face off in just the third all-American men's US Open semifinal this century.

In the other semifinal, top-ranked Alexander Zverev will take on unseeded Karen Khachanov.

From top storylines to analysis, we've got you covered with everything you need ahead of Friday's play.

Alexander Zverev enters the semifinal looking to reach his third consecutive major final.

Since playing consecutive five-set matches to begin the tournament, Zverev has regained top form, finding his angles on serve while continuing to find success with his improved forehand.

Meanwhile, Karen Khachanov enters as the lowest-ranked US Open semifinalist since Grigor Dimitrov in 2019.

Khachanov has struggled to find his form throughout the year.

The former top-10 player did not win any matches during the hard-court swing leading up to the US Open.

However, he's always consistently demonstrated the ability to elevate his performance in Grand Slams.

Zverev enters as the well-deserved favorite, considering he has reached consecutive major finals.

That being said, opportunities like these surely don't come often for Khachanov, and if he can find his forehand early, he can make this a difficult match.

On Friday, Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe will stride onto Arthur Ashe Stadium for a rare showdown: just the third all-American men's US Open semifinal of this century.

Both players arrive with serious momentum after impressive victories.

Tiafoe staged an improbable comeback, clawing his way back from two sets down to defeat Alex Michelsen.

Shelton, meanwhile, finally slayed goliath, toppling reigning champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set classic that finished at 3:33 a.m., the latest conclusion in US Open history.

The 23-year-old is playing the best tennis of his life.

His thunderous serve can top 150 MPH, but it is his ability to blend relentless offense with gritty defense that truly sets him apart.

Tiafoe, meanwhile, has always found his groove during the American hard-court swing.

Now in his third US Open semifinal, the 28-year-old is looking to break through and reach his first major final.

Like Shelton, he can dominate with his serve and forehand.

For Tiafoe, a fast start will be crucial because Shelton has not eased up throughout the tournament.

This clash promises fireworks, but with Shelton's current momentum, he appears to have a slight edge.

Either way, fans should expect a thriller.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Britons Joe Salisbury and Henry Patten into men's doubles semi-finals
articles.summary: Three-time US Open doubles champions Joe Salisbury and Rajeev Ram beat last year's winners Marcel Granollers and Horacio Zeballos to reach the semi-finals.
articles.body:
Reunited three-time US Open men's doubles champions Joe Salisbury and Rajeev Ram knocked out last year's winners Marcel Granollers and Horacio Zeballos to reach the semi-finals.

Britain's Salisbury won the title at at Flushing Meadows in New York alongside American Ram in 2021, 2022 and 2023, but they split in 2024 before teaming up again this year.

They won 6-4 6-4 against the second seeds and will face 2024 runners-up Kevin Krawietz and Tim Putz from Germany on Thursday.

In the other half of the draw, Briton Henry Patten and Finn Harri Heliovaara saved three match points on their way to a 6-7 (7-9) 7-6 (7-3) 6-2 triumph over seventh seeds Manuel Guinard and Guido Andreozzi.

Wimbledon champions and top seeds Patten and Heliovaara spurned four set points in the opening set and had to stave off match points in the second.

They will meet Briton Neal Skupski and American Christian Harrison, who beat Simone Bolelli and Andrea Vavassori 6-3 6-2 in the last quarter-final.

In the women's doubles, top seeds Katerina Siniakova, from the Czech Republic, and American Taylor Townsend are one victory away from lifting all four Grand Slam titles together after winning 6-0 7-6 (10-8) against Diana Shnaider and Elise Mertens.

They will contest Friday's final with Americans Robin Montgomery and Ashlyn Krueger, who saved three match points and came from 8-2 down in the match tie-break to beat second seeds Luisa Stefani and Gabriella Dabrowski 4-6 6-4 7-6 (10-8).

articles.title: US Open winner Andy Roddick defends late finishes amid criticism after Ben Shelton-Carlos Alcaraz thriller
articles.summary: Andy Roddick defended the US Open's late-night scheduling on his "Served" podcast after Ben Shelton's epic win over Carlos Alcaraz ended at 3:33 a.m.
articles.body: Retired American tennis star Andy Roddick weighed in on Ben Shelton’s five-set victory over Carlos Alcaraz at the U.S. Open, which ended in the early hours of Wednesday morning. Shelton secured the biggest victory of his young professional career in a tiebreaker shortly after 3:30 a.m. ET, becoming the first American man to defeat either Alcaraz or Jannik Sinner at a Grand Slam. His victory, coupled with Frances Tiafoe’s five-set win over fellow American Alex Michelsen in the other men’s quarterfinal, guaranteed that at least one American would reach the 2026 U.S. Open final. The last time an American-born man brought home the men's singles title at the U.S. Open was in 2003, when Roddick won his lone Grand Slam. On a recent edition of his "Served" podcast, Roddick addressed criticism surrounding the tournament's late-night schedule and overall logistics, making clear he had no regrets about how the match ultimately turned out. NOVAK DJOKOVIC SUFFERS STUNNING DEFEAT IN FIRST ROUND OF US OPEN AFTER TRYING TO BATTLE THROUGH AILMENTS "I know a lot of the comments are, you know, ‘How do you finish at four in the morning?’ and all of that," Roddick said. "Well, every match goes to a match tiebreak except for one. And you’ve got to get 25,000 people out of a stadium responsibly, and you’ve got to get 25,000 people in responsibly. So, I hear a lot of complaining. I don’t hear a lot of proposed solutions." Roddick stood by the Grand Slam's late-night session format while conceding that a five-hour match could test viewers’ patience, echoing a concern raised by sports podcaster Bill Simmons. "Starting earlier wasn’t possible because of Frances and Mickelson’s match," Roddick said. "And so, you have to have a night session at the US Open. It’s one of the things that we all love. And they’ve been on the wrong side of luck. Now, I know there are some people who have said shorter format. And I know Bill Simmons made the point that this is ridiculous, that we’re playing too long. He’s normally well-thought-out in his thoughts. I don’t disagree with the premise that, like, ‘Five hours is too much. I’m bored.'" THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "7-6 in the fifth last night for Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz in that match, where Tiafoe is down two sets, and the guy’s serving for it — I kind of like the fact that we have a sport where you get into these long-form matches, and it’s the hardest thing on earth," Roddick said. "It’s the hardest sport in the world. If you take that away, can we lay that claim anymore? I don’t know." Roddick acknowledged the practical case for a shorter format, noting the challenges a late-night match can pose for those working behind the scenes. "I understand all the pragmatists out there that say we should have a shorter format. I understand the reasons for it. I understand that it’s inconvenient for Sean to be up until 4:00 a.m., you know, watching this match while he’s editing last night’s show," Roddick said. "I understand that some people have to go to sleep because, like you, I had to go to sleep to protect my workday today. I understand all of the rational arguments." articles.title: Zverev pasa a las semifinales del US Open tras 16 horas y 40 minutos
articles.standfirst: El alemán derrota por la vía rápida a Van de Zandschulp y se las verá este viernes con Khachanov
articles.summary: El alemán derrota por la vía rápida a Van de Zandschulp y se las verá este viernes con Khachanov
articles.body: Por quinto día seguido, por el simple hecho de que le gusta dormir, Alexander Zverev cerró la jornada del US Open. Y por quinto día sumó una victoria que le clasifica para las semifinales del último grande del curso. Su última víctima fue Botic van de Zandschulp, por 6-2, 7-5 y 6-1. El alemán ha necesitado 16 horas y 40 minutos para meterse entre los cuatro mejores, una cantidad de tiempo que no se veía desde la edición de 1991. Sascha, al que le gusta acostarse tarde y levantarse también tarde, confesó en medio de la central Arthur Ashe que fue uno más delante del televisor el martes siguiendo los cuartos de final que protagonizaron Carlos Alcaraz y Ben Shelton: "Estuve levantado hasta las tres porque sabía que me iba a levantar igualmente a la una del mediodía". Zvetev, que ha hecho valer su condición de primer favorito del cuadro, se cruzará este viernes con Karen Khachanov por un puesto en la final. Está a dos victorias de sumar más grandes (2) este curso que Jannik Sinner y Alcaraz. El italiano y el español se conforman con uno. El tenista de Hamburgo, flamante campeón de Roland Garros, está lejos de poder inquietar el número 1 mundial de Jannik Sinner. La diferencia entre ambos es de 3.010 puntos. Sin embargo distancia un poco más a Alcaraz, que está hoy a 2.930 puntos.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Alexander Zverev storms into semi-finals despite late bedtime
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev storms into the US Open last four despite staying up until 3:30am to watch Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz's blockbuster quarter-final.
articles.body:
Alexander Zverev booked his place in the US Open semi-finals with a commanding victory over Botic van de Zandschulp - despite staying up until 3:30am to watch Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz's blockbuster quarter-final.

The top seed swept aside the Dutchman with a 6-2 7-5 6-1 win in the night session on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Following his victory, Zverev revealed he had stayed up to watch Shelton's win over defending champion Alcaraz in a match that ended at 03:34 local time on Wednesday - the latest finish in the tournament's history.

"I watched Shelton-Alcaraz until 3.30am last night," Zverev said.

"I did not go to bed, I was up late, I was watching TV because I was sleeping in until 1pm anyway."

The 29-year-old has had plenty of his own late-night finishes at this year's tournament, with his opening three matches ending at 1:55am, 2:15am and 1:09am.

Bidding to reach a third successive Grand Slam final, Zverev will face Russian Karen Khachanov, who advanced after Alexander Blockx retired trailing 6-2 7-5 3-2.

With his win over Van de Zandschulp, Zverev has reached all four Grand Slam semi-finals in a single season for the first time in his career.

"I think the more often that you get to that stage, the more normal it becomes, which is something that you should never take for granted," said Zverev, who ended his wait for a maiden major at this year's French Open.

"I think it's a very special feeling when it becomes normality."

Gauff saves match points to set up Rybakina semi-final

'Just a number' - Rybakina's rise to world number one

Hewett and Reid into last eight of US Open singles

Zverev is the favourite to win the title following Alcaraz's exit, although it has taken time to reach his best level in New York.

The German was taken to five sets in his opening two matches, while he has conceded 80 games at this year's tournament - the second most of any top seed en route to the semi-finals after only Rafael Nadal, who lost 85 games in 2018.

"I think you saw in the first two rounds, I really didn't play well," Zverev said.

"In other tournaments I would be out in the first round, but here I can fight back and play best of five sets, play four-and-a-half hours. I've started playing better throughout the tournament and I'm definitely happy to be in the semi-finals here."

Zverev has won 23 singles matches at majors in 2026 - the most by a German man in a single season, surpassing Boris Becker's 22 in 1989.

Blockx run ruined by injury as 'Professor' Khachanov progresses

Blockx's dream run in New York ended in cruel fashion earlier on Wednesday as the Belgian was forced to retire after suffering a series of injuries in his quarter-final against Khachanov.

Playing in his first Grand Slam quarter-final, the 21-year-old first received medical treatment for a blister on his foot before struggling with a back issue.

"I think today my body just gave up," said Blockx, who had come close to retiring from his fourth-round win against Francisco Cerundolo with a rib injury.

"During the match, it was quite funny to me. I just had to laugh it off because it was just something new the whole time.

"I felt it was getting worse and worse. I couldn't land without feeling pain, without feeling my back, my ribs. So I just didn't want to yeah, maybe make it worse to miss the entire season."

Khachanov wished Blockx a "speedy recovery" after he secured his place in a Grand Slam semi-final for the first time since the Australian Open in 2023.

A former world number eight, a disappointing run of results over the past few months have resulted in Khachanov's ranking dipping to 50 and he is unseeded at a major for the first time since 2018.

The 30-year-old said he will have to come up with his "best form" to defeat Zverev and reach his first major final.

"He's been in the top five for so many years. This year he did also step forward. He won his first Grand Slam, played the final in Wimbledon, as well. He's coming up really in hot form," Khachanov said.

Zverev, meanwhile, says he will have to be wary of his opponent and his extensive knowledge of the game.

"We call him [Khachanov] 'The Professor', actually, because he knows everything about tennis, and he knows every single string tension, knows what everybody does, so that's quite fun," Zverev said.

articles.title: Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi’s loss ends India’s junior singles challenge
articles.summary: Tennis News: New York City: India’s Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi, the 15th seed, saved four match points after fighting back from a set and a break down in the decide.
articles.body: New York City: India’s Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi, the 15th seed, saved four match points after fighting back from a set and a break down in the decider, but could not complete the comeback, going down 3-6, 7-5, 5-7 to Russian qualifier Arina Malygina in two hours and 16 minutes in the US Open girls’ singles second round.Malygina, ranked 104, has an unorthodox game. The 18-year-old uses a generous dose of underspin from the back of the court, chipping her returns and taking pace off the ball whenever the rallies pick up, before suddenly producing some clean ball-striking of her own.Maaya, 17, doesn’t hold back. She likes to go for her shots, a strategy that is likely to pay off when she plays the pros, but in the juniors there is always the risk that the error count keeps climbing.On Tuesday, Maaya was clocking upwards of 110 mph on her first serve for most of the match, but also had 10 double faults. She fought back from 1-3 and 3-5 in the third set, with all five of Malygina’s match points coming on Maaya’s serve, two in the 10th game and three in the 12th.“I felt like my level dropped today. She played great, I don’t want to take anything away from her. She found ways to win the match,” Maaya said.“She played important points better than me. It was a very close match and whoever managed to handle that situation better would come through, she did that better than me.”She added, “I should have gone for my serves in the third set, the speed dropped to 95 mph in some games.”Meanwhile, in the boys’ doubles, India’s Arnav Paparkar and Thailand’s Kunanan Pantaratorn fell to American Safir Azam and Kazakhstan’s Damir Zhalgasbay 4-6, 2-6.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: US Open: Alexander Zverev passes Botic van de ​Zandschulp test to set up semi-final date with Karen Khachanov
articles.summary: Top seed Alexander Zverev ‌through to semi-finals where he will take on Karen Khachanov; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The 29-year-old French Open champion and Wimbledon runner-up got off to a slow start in his campaign at Flushing ​Meadows but has steadily found his range.

Zverev played five-set matches in each of the first two matches, but he has won his last three in straight sets and is the only man to reach all four Grand Slam semi-finals this year.

Into his 13th major semi-final, Zverev will face Karen Khachanov in the last four for a spot in Sunday's final.

"I ‌think you saw in the first two rounds, I really didn't play well," said Zverev, who has spent 16 hours and 40 minutes on court, the most by any man en route to the semi-finals at the US Open since 1991.

"In other tournaments I would be out in the first round, but here I can fight back and play best of ​five sets, play four-and-a-half hours. I've started playing ⁠better throughout the tournament and I'm ⁠definitely happy to be in the semi-finals here."

The German was far from steady on serve early ‌on at Arthur Ashe Stadium, coughing up five double faults in an erratic start, but Dutchman Van de Zandschulp leaked forehand errors to ‌allow the top seed to break in the fifth game and then take the first set.

Van de Zandschulp regrouped in the second set and came close to levelling the contest, but Zverev absorbed ⁠the pressure and reeled off three games in a ​row towards the end as the momentum ​swung firmly in the German's favour.

Zverev, the 2020 runner-up, fired ​an overhead smash to break early in the third ⁠set and cruised home from there to reach his third semi-final in New York.

Khachanov back to semi-finals with walkover

Khachanov advanced to the semi-finals when Alexander Blockx retired trailing 6-2 7-5 3-2, as the world No 50 reached the final-four stage in Flushing Meadows for ‌the first time since 2022.

Blockx, who became the first Belgian man to reach the quarter-finals here, was already carrying a rib injury into the match and was visibly hampered by further physical issues.

He wore a ​brace on his right ankle and had his thigh wrapped, ‌with the 21-year-old also calling for the trainer during the contest.

Khachanov will return to a Grand Slam semi-final for the first time since reaching the ⁠last four at the Australian Open in 2023.

"I was preparing really ​well for that match-up; it's not easy because ​I feel I was dominating then I felt he was struggling more ​and more," Khachanov said on court.

"He was suffering, but I wanted to keep ⁠the energy there. I wish him a speedy recovery but I'm super happy I'm in the semis."

The US Open is live on Sky Sports from August 30. Stream tennis with no contract on NOW and the Sky Sports App . You can also watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports.

articles.title: McEnroe, sobre Alcaraz: "Mi favorito. ¿Cómo demonios puede estar tan feliz en la cancha?"
articles.standfirst: El extenista aseguró en una entrevista que "disfruta cada minuto. Espero que tenga un futuro brillante. Es increíble para nuestro deporte y tiene una personalidad fantástica"
articles.summary: El extenista aseguró en una entrevista que "disfruta cada minuto. Espero que tenga un futuro brillante. Es increíble para nuestro deporte y tiene una personalidad fantástica"
articles.body: Después de más de cuatro meses alejado de las pistas por una lesión en la muñeca, Carlos Alcaraz regresó al circuito a un grandísimo nivel, pese a su derrota en cuartos ante Ben Shelton, en un agónico encuentro que se decidió en el súper 'tie-break', por 5-7(5), 6-1, 6-3 y 7-6(7). El español, que estuvo en pista hasta las 3.35 de la madrugada y tras 4 horas y 28 minutos de juego, hizo un balance positivo tras el partido, del que se fue con una sonrisa tras agradecer al público su apoyo durante el torneo. "Me voy con la cabeza alta, contento y sano. He jugado contra una bestia. Tengo ganas de volver a casa y entrenar para lo que me queda. A veces se gana y a veces se pierde", reflexionaba tras la derrota. Y precisamente ese talante es el que ha destacado John McEnroe, que se deshizo en elogios para el tenista español. "Veo a Alcaraz en pista y me pregunto cómo demonios puede estar tan feliz en la cancha todo el tiempo. Siempre he pensado que disfruta cada minuto y segundo en pista", aseguró el legendario exjugador en una entrevista en 'Tennis Insider Club'. El exnúmero uno del mundo insistió en que el español es su "jugador favorito" por cómo maneja la presión y su estilo de juego: "Me encanta Alcaraz, es mi jugador favorito. Simplemente, no puedo creer que este chico pueda ser así, es asombroso".

articles.title: US Open 2026: Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff & Elena Rybakina make up historic semi-final line-up
articles.summary: For the first time since 1975, the top four seeds in the women's US Open singles draw have reached the semi-finals.
articles.body:
That was Coco Gauff's surprised reaction when she learned she was part of a US Open semi-final line-up that has not been seen in more than half a century.

For the first time since 1975, the top four seeds in the women's singles draw have reached the semi-finals at the New York major.

Now, 51 years later, the stars have aligned once again with Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula and Gauff all surviving three-set thrillers to create a semi-final line-up for the ages.

"How amazing - it doesn't get much better than that does it?," former British number one Annabel Croft told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"It has felt fantastic the whole tournament - I just feel like I've been more enthused about looking forward to the match-ups this Grand Slam than any I can remember."

It is the first time the top-four ranked players have reached the women's semi-finals at any Grand Slam since Wimbledon in 2009, and it hints at a shift away from the unpredictable landscape that has characterised the women's game in recent years.

Since the start of 2020, there have been 13 different Grand Slam women's singles champions - compared to just seven on the men's side.

"I just feel like there's lots of really big names now, big personalities going up against each other and it's really exciting," Croft added.

"We've been blessed with the amount of intriguing matches we've had. You're seeing these warriors out on court."

Top seed and two-time defending champion Sabalenka will face American Pegula in Thursday's first semi-final (00:00 BST, Friday), while Rybakina - who will replace Sabalenka as the new world number one on Monday - takes on fourth seed Gauff afterwards.

'It's a battle, it's a fight' - Sabalenka-Pegula rivalry continues

While Sabalenka is bidding to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2014 to win three successive US Open titles, Pegula is the only player remaining in the women's draw still chasing a maiden Grand Slam.

The pair need no introduction to each other, having faced each other 13 times.

That includes the past two US Open tournaments, when Sabalenka denied Pegula a first major title in the 2024 final and fought back to win in last year's semi-finals.

"It's fun to look at it like a rivalry. I think that's what motivates me," said Pegula.

"I know that she's definitely pushed me to become a better player, so I always respect and appreciate that aspect of our rivalry."

Pegula, who has got the better of Sabalenka on four occasions on the WTA Tour, said beating the four-time major winner at Grand Slam level is a "hurdle" she must overcome.

Sabalenka, meanwhile, said she was "super excited" to face Pegula, who arrived in New York in better form after reaching the final in both Washington and Cincinnati.

"I'm loving playing against her because it's a battle, because it's a fight, and I love being under pressure and going through tough challenges," said Sabalenka, who is into her first semi-final since falling to Pegula at June's Berlin Open.

"I know she hasn't maybe had the best results this summer, but I know that she has a lot of confidence playing here at this tournament, and she's going for a three-peat," Pegula added.

'Different mindset and perspective' aids Gauff

By reaching the semi-finals, second seed Rybakina will become the new world number one on Monday - ending Sabalenka's 99-week reign at the top.

But the second seed has described the top ranking as "just a number" and stressed that her focus remains focused on winning her third Grand Slam title.

"It's never quite the same if you become world number one having lost a Grand Slam final or semi-final just beforehand, so she will be trying to cap off an absolutely perfect couple of weeks by winning the title," tennis correspondent Russell Fuller said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

Standing in her way, however, is Gauff, who will have the home crowd's backing on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The 22-year-old American, who won the Flushing Meadows title in 2023 but suffered fourth-round exits in the following two years, said she has a different perspective to this year's tournament.

"Sometimes you're just so focused on the now, now, now, because you want it now, and obviously you want to take advantage of your opportunities," she said.

"In the grand scheme of things, [I'm] definitely sitting here in a different mindset and perspective than I was last year.

"It inspires me a little bit more to keep working, as I see how much I have improved in a year."

Gauff leads the head-to-head 2-1, but Australian Open champion Rybakina fought back from a set down to triumph in last month's Canadian Open semi-finals.

"I'm going to have some aces hit on me and some winners hit on me, but I'm going to keep fighting and give it my all. That's all I can do," Gauff said.

articles.title: Same height, similar age, vastly different paths: Zverev and Khachanov eye US Open final
articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW YORK CITY: They are the same height, almost the same age, and go back a long way, both have spent years knocking on the door of Grand Slam success.
articles.body: NEW YORK CITY: They are the same height, almost the same age, and go back a long way, both have spent years knocking on the door of Grand Slam success. Standing at 6 ft 6’, there’s little to separate Alexander Zverev and Karen Khachanov physically when they meet in the US Open semi-finals on Friday. But the German arrives as the top seed, Olympic gold medallist and now a major champion, while Khachanov, the world No. 50, is chasing a first Slam final.Zverev, 29, has already been here before. He reached the US Open final in 2020 and came within two points of the title before Dominic Thiem turned the match around in a five-set battle. Almost four years later, he reached the final at Roland Garros and followed it up with another Grand Slam final at Melbourne Park in 2025, but was still waiting for his first Slam crown. The lanky German finally flipped the script in Paris in June, claiming his maiden Slam title before reaching the final again at Wimbledon.The top seed booked his place in the last four with a commanding 6-2, 7-5, 6-1 win over Botic van de Zandschulp. It is his 13th Grand Slam semi-final, second only among active men to Novak Djokovic’s 55, and his 51st match win of the season, the most on the ATP Tour.The first of the last-four clashes on Friday will be an all-American affair, world No.9 Ben Shelton, the conqueror of Carlos Alcaraz, will play the 12th ranked Frances Tiafoe, with Shelton leading the head-to-head 3-1. Both men are looking to make their first major final.For Khachanov, the road back to the last four has been considerably more arduous. The 30-year-old arrived in New York ranked No. 50 after going 16-18 through the first eight months of the season, his lowest ranking since May 2017. He has since beaten American Learner Tien in five sets and reached the semi-finals when Alexander Blockx retired with an upper-body injury while trailing 6-2, 7-5, 3-2.It is the Russian’s third Grand Slam semi-final and his second in New York, after his run to the last four in 2022. He also reached the Australian Open semi-finals in 2023. But the next step has remained elusive.“Every Grand Slam, every big stage, you want to do well. This is what we've been dreaming of as a kid, you know, to play on the further stages of this event, that one day it can come,” Khachanov said. “That's why I think it's a little bit a moment of appreciation, and at the same time, ambition and motivation for what's coming next.”What comes next is an opponent who has had the better of him over the years.Zverev leads their head-to-head 6-3, including his victory over Khachanov in the 2021 Tokyo Olympics gold-medal match. Khachanov did, however, beat him in Canada last year, a win that came after several defeats to the German.“He is where he is, because he deserves to be there,” Khachanov said. “He's been in top 5 for so many years. This year he also took a step forward. He won his first Grand Slam. He's in hot form.”The numbers tell only part of the story. Both men can generate huge pace from the baseline, both possess formidable serves and neither is likely to give ground easily. Khachanov knows that against Zverev, patience will be as important as power.“I will have to come up with the best form,” he said. “I will have to have patience.”Zverev and Khachanov go back a long time to their junior days.“People don't see from the outside, but he's somebody that works extremely hard. He's on the practice courts more than most people. He's always searching for solutions. He's always, you know, trying to find new ways to get better,” Zverev said of Khachanov, one of the more popular figures in the locker-room. “I have massive respect for him. I hope it's going to be a great battle.”For Zverev, the prize is another chance to finish what he started in New York six years ago. For Khachanov, it is an opportunity to reach a Grand Slam final for the first time.Meanwhile in the girls doubles second round, Maaya and Antonina Sushkova of Ukraine upset the fifth-seeded combine, Czechs Jana Kovackova and Katerina Zajickova on 2-6, 6-2, 10-7.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Hasta Ginóbili entra en el debate por los horarios del tenis: "¿Es necesario jugar al mejor de cinco sets?"
articles.standfirst: Los jerarcas del tenis estudian la opción de reducir los partidos para no perder aficionados
articles.summary: Los jerarcas del tenis estudian la opción de reducir los partidos para no perder aficionados
articles.body: Se suele decir que cuando el río suena agua lleva. En 2012, la final del Open de Australia, entre Rafael Nadal y Novak Djokovic, marcó un antes y un después en el tenis. Estuvo muy bien el espectáculo, pero las 05.53 minutos de parido hicieron replantear las reglas a los jerarcas del tenis. Desde entonces se aceleró el juego, con el reloj de tiempo en el saque, en el calentamiento... La obsesión era no perder aficionados y que estos se marcharan a otras disciplinas deportivas donde sabes cuándo empieza un partido y cuándo termina. No es el caso del tenis y mucho menos en los Grand Slam donde los enfrentamientos siguen siendo al mejor de cinco sets. Andrew Abdo, el nuevo CEO del Open de Australia, en sustitución de Craig Tiley, que se ha movido al US Open, ya ha abierto la posibilidad del cambio: "Quizá no juguemos al mejor de cinco sets en los Grand Slam del futuro" Esa idea es compartida por deportistas de renombre mundial como el argentino Manu Ginóbili. "¿Realmente necesitan los Grand Slam ser al mejor de cinco sets? Cinco horas se siente una locura para los jugadores, incluso para los fans", escribía en sus redes sociales. El debate está abierto. Feliciano López, director del Mutua Madrid Open y de las Finales de la Copa Davis de Bolonia, está estos días en Nueva York como comentarista de televisión. En su caso es un defensor de los cinco sets y lo hizo evidente tras el duelo entre Alcaraz y Shelton que terminó a altas horas de la madrugada: "Larga vida a los 5 sets. Una pena que uno tenga que perder, el tenis es cruel pero fascinante a la vez. Carlitos está sano! Gracias a todos los valientes que esta pasada madrugada nos habéis acompañado". Tanto Alcaraz como Shelton mostraron su sorpresa que en un día laboral la grada de la central de Nueva York no se despoblara. Fue una excepción y las mentes pensantes del tenis buscan atraer a las nuevas generaciones. Con partidos tan largos no lo van a conseguir. La ATP ya tomó en 2007 una controvertida decisión en 2007. Y fue la de eliminar las finales de Masters 1000 al mejor de cinco mangas, al igual que la de las ATP Finals. La razón oficial para ello fue lo cargado del calendario.

articles.title: US Open Tennis 2026 TV Schedule and Women's Semifinal Bracket Predictions
articles.summary: Thursday's US Open women's semifinals will showcase the very best in tennis.
articles.body:
Thursday's US Open women's semifinals will showcase the very best in tennis.

Remarkably, this is the first time since 1975 that all four top-seeded women have reached the semifinals.

Aryna Sabalenka is aiming for a rare three-peat, while Jessica Pegula is still seeking that first major title.

Meanwhile, Coco Gauff is chasing another US Open title, while Elena Rybakina looks to extend her dominant season.

From match times to ultimate predictions, we've got you covered with everything you need below.

Time: 7 p.m. ET (Sabalenka vs. Pegula), 8:30 p.m. (Rybakina vs. Gauff)

Aryna Sabalenka just faced her toughest test yet, battling past Linda Noskova in a thrilling three-set quarterfinal.

Now, the world No. 1 is only two wins away from becoming just the third woman in the Open Era (since 1968) to win three consecutive US Open titles.

Jessica Pegula, however, is determined to end that streak and possibly seek some revenge in the process.

Sabalenka has gotten the better of Pegula in their last two US Open meetings, including a dramatic 2024 final and another win in the 2025 semifinal.

This time, Pegula comes in with plenty of momentum after her own hard-fought victory, rallying from a slow start to defeat fellow American Emma Navarro.

She has put together an impressive run so far, finding her groove at the baseline and dominating with her first serve.

The question is whether Pegula can pull off the upset.

For her to move on, she will need to cut down on early unforced errors and establish her first serve from the start.

There is no doubt she is physically up for the challenge.

However, with so much history on the line, Sabalenka is likely to raise her level and push for her eighth straight hard-court Grand Slam final, which would match Monica Seles for the longest streak ever by a woman.

Prediction: No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka def. No. 3 Jessica Pegula in 3 sets

Elena Rybakina, already a two-time Grand Slam champion, is aiming to become the sixth woman since 1988 to win both hardcourt majors in the same year.

She has looked nearly unstoppable this tournament, dropping only one set on her way to the semifinals.

Coco Gauff has been in top form as well.

The 22-year-old American comes into this match on an 11-match winning streak.

Gauff was pushed in the opening set of her quarterfinal but found her best tennis late to get past Mirra Andreeva.

For Gauff, a strong start is crucial, particularly after her slow opening against Andreeva.

She is known as one of the best returners on the tour, but against a server and baseline powerhouse like Rybakina, she needs to find her rhythm early.

Service breaks will be rare, so every chance will matter.

If Gauff can make the match a physical contest and force Rybakina into long rallies, there is no reason why her US Open run can't continue.

Prediction: No. 4 Coco Gauff def. No. 2 Elena Rybakina in 3 sets

articles.title: Coco Gauff’s controversial tennis style gets strong defense from Serena Williams’ coach after US Open comeback
articles.summary: International Sports News: Rick Macci has pushed back at critics who call Coco Gauff’s tennis “ugly,” arguing that style should not matter as much as what a player can do when a.
articles.body: Rick Macci has pushed back at critics who call Coco Gauff’s tennis “ugly,” arguing that style should not matter as much as what a player can do when a match gets tough. The longtime coach, who worked with Serena Williams and Venus Williams, defended Gauff after her comeback win over Mirra Andreeva at the 2026 US Open. His point was simple: tennis is about winning points, not looking perfect.Rick Macci defends Coco Gauff’s “ugly” tennis after Mirra Andreeva comebackMacci shared his thoughts on X after Gauff reached the US Open semifinals. “Many people chirp that Coco and her game is ugly. Trust me they are looking at the wrong movie. This is not a beauty contest or a ballroom dancing. Tennis at the highest level is WHAT IS UNDER THE HOOD,” he wrote.“Many players can make the sport flowing and glowing like the great FED,” Macci wrote. “Coco checks so many athletic boxes inside and out and always ready for a 15 round bout.”That view fits what happened against Andreeva. Gauff lost the first set 6-2 and looked uncomfortable. She made 42 unforced errors and hit 12 double faults, according to the official US Open match statistics. Still, she stayed in the match long enough to change its direction.The biggest moment came in the second-set tiebreak. Andreeva had two match points, but Gauff saved both and took the set. She then pulled away in the deciding set to win 2-6, 7-6(7), 6-2 and reach the semifinals for the second time in her career.That is where Macci’s “under the hood” point becomes important. Gauff can use her speed to reach balls many players would give up on, keep rallies alive and wait for a chance to take control. It may not always look clean, but it can be hard to break down.Coco Gauff’s coaching changes add another layer to her gameGauff currently works with Jean-Christophe Faurel and biomechanics specialist Gavin MacMillan, who joined her team in August 2025 after she parted ways with Matt Daly.MacMillan was brought in mainly to help with Gauff’s serve. He had previously worked with Aryna Sabalenka on the same part of her game. The move came after serve problems, including 23 double faults against Danielle Collins in Montreal and 16 in her Cincinnati quarterfinal loss to Jasmine Paolini.She had shown the value of a new coaching voice during her 2023 run with Brad Gilbert, winning in Washington, Cincinnati and New York.Daly had joined Gauff after the 2024 US Open, and their partnership brought quick success, with Gauff winning the China Open and WTA Finals. MacMillan’s arrival was therefore another major change, even though Gauff had already been winning big titles.Now, another test awaits there. Gauff will face Elena Rybakina in the US Open semifinals. Rybakina reached the last four by beating Zheng Qinwen and also secured the world No. 1 ranking. Gauff may not always produce the prettiest tennis, but she has again shown why results can matter more than appearance.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: All About Jessica Pegula’s 4 Siblings
articles.summary: Jessica Pegula and her brothers, Michael and Matthew, and sisters, Kelly and Laura, are the children of billionaire Terry Pegula
articles.body:
Jessica Pegula has two brothers and two sisters

Laura Pegula, a former collegiate tennis player, inspired Jessica to pursue the sport

Kelly Pegula saved their mother's life in 2022 by performing CPR during a cardiac arrest emergency

Jessica Pegula 's four siblings — Michael, Laura, Kelly and Matthew —have rooted for her as she competes in the 2026 US Open .

"My siblings always love coming," she told Town & Country in August 2025 ahead of the US Open, which she said they frequented as kids. "They love being in the city and just being a part of it and it is always really fun ... there's just a lot more a personal attachment to it than maybe the other ones."

The tennis star's dad, billionaire Terry Pegula , welcomed Michael and Laura during a previous marriage before he wed her mom, Kim Pegula , in 1993. Jessica was born a year later, followed by Kelly and Matthew.

Terry built the family's fortune through natural gas and petroleum, later expanding into sports ownership with Kim. Together, they own the NFL's Buffalo Bills and the NHL's Buffalo Sabres. However, his second-eldest daughter has made a name for herself in tennis, emerging as one of the top American players in the sport by reaching the quarterfinals in all four Grand Slams. In 2024, she broke through to her first Grand Slam final at the US Open.

After her semifinal win, Jessica thanked her supporters, including her siblings, in an on-court interview for being by her side: "I have so much family here, and they have been watching a lot of my matches, so to still be here and have them still here supporting me is crazy. I am glad that they are able to share this moment with me."

Here's everything to know about Jessica Pegula's siblings: Michael, Laura, Kelly and Matthew.

Michael is nearly 20 years older than Jessica

Michael is the eldest of Terry's children from a previous marriage and has largely stayed out of the public eye. When Terry married Kim in 1993, Michael was 16, and his younger sister Laura was 11.

The couple settled in Orchard Park, N.Y., to stay close to the children, who lived nearby with their mother. Blending families during the teenage years wasn't without challenges, and Kim has been candid about the adjustment period.

"Obviously divorce on kids is always hard — especially when you're in those teen years, and you're going through a bunch of other things," she told Buffalo Magazine in May 2015. "But I knew what I was getting into. You just have to spend the time with them. Kids get older and start seeing things differently. And time heals everything."

Athletic talent runs in the Pegula family, and Laura carved out her own space on the court long before Jessica turned pro.

Laura graduated from North Allegheny High School in Pennsylvania in 2000, where she proved herself a standout player. She then played collegiate tennis at the University of Pittsburgh.

During her time with the Panthers, she became a valuable contributor and was named the team's Most Valuable Player one year.

Jessica has credited her sister with introducing her to the sport.

"My older sister, Laura, played Division I tennis, so I was always around it and followed in her footsteps," she told Elle in March 2025.

In June 2022, the Pegula family faced an emergency when Kim suffered a sudden cardiac arrest while sleeping. It was Kelly, Jessica's younger sister, who acted quickly in a moment that saved Kim's life.

Staying at her parents' home that night, Kelly performed CPR on her unresponsive mother until paramedics arrived.

Jessica later shared just how close the call was, praising her sister's actions in those critical minutes.

"Even though she doesn't like to take credit for this terrible situation, she absolutely saved her life," she wrote in an essay for The Players' Tribune in February 2023.

Kelly had completed her CPR certification only a few months earlier for a job requirement.

Matthew is the youngest of the Pegula kids. Though he's mostly remained private, he has stepped out to support Jessica at tennis tournaments, including at the Ecotrans Ladies Open Berlin in June 2024, and joined his mom during her first public appearance after her cardiac arrest.

Laura is part of the Buffalo Bills management team

Following Kim's 2022 cardiac arrest and ongoing recovery, the Pegula family quietly began making long-term plans for the future of their NFL franchise.

In 2023, Terry transferred a small percentage of the Buffalo Bills to his daughter Laura, who was long involved in the family petroleum business, signaling her growing role in the organization.

According to The Athletic , the move was made to comply with the NFL's succession planning policy, which requires each team to designate a successor in case the controlling owner dies or becomes incapacitated.

Terry, who became Kim's legal guardian after her health crisis, placed many of her assets in a trust, and soon after, formally named Laura as part of the ownership structure.

Laura has since taken on a more active role on the team and was part of the committee searching for the Bills' new head coach in January 2026, per Buffalo Rumblings .

Jessica and Kelly once owned a health food business

In 2016, Jessica and Kelly launched The Healthy Scratch, a quick-service restaurant in Buffalo, N.Y., offering smoothies, cold-pressed juices, salads, acai bowls and wraps.

After the original location opened, the brand quickly expanded, adding a food truck in 2017, followed by café locations inside medical buildings. They also opened a grab-and-go setup inside a local cycling studio.

The Healthy Scratch ran for six years before closing its final locations in May 2022, according to WGRZ .

articles.title: Alcaraz puso una revolucionaria máquina a disposición de Granollers para poder jugar los cuartos
articles.standfirst: El barcelonés sufrió un fuerte esguince en su tobillo derecho y fue a tratarse a la habitación de Carlitos
articles.summary: El barcelonés sufrió un fuerte esguince en su tobillo derecho y fue a tratarse a la habitación de Carlitos
articles.body: Por muchas razones Carlos Alcaraz es el tenista más querido en los vestuarios del circuito y también en las gradas de todos los puntos del planeta donde juega. Un ejemplo de ello es el episodio que sucedió la tarde del martes y que MARCA ha conocido. Marcel Granollers, uno de los mejores doblistas del mundo, se hizo un esguince de tobillo en su pie derecho durante el partido de octavos del US Open contra los argentinos Molteni y González. Junto a otro argentino, Horacio Zeballos, acabaron ganando y pasando a cuartos. La organización había programado su siguiente compromiso el miércoles y Marcel tenía apenas 24 horas para intentar recuperar su maltrecho tobillo que lucía completamente hinchado como una pelota. Fue entonces cuando coincidió en los vestuarios de la Arthur Ashe con Alcaraz, que venía de calentar para su duelo de cuartos de la sesión nocturna con Ben Shelton. Al conocer la lesión de su compañero le ofreció tratarse con una revolucionaria máquina con la que viaja que tiene una tecnología de radiofrecuencia no invasiva que opera a una frecuencia fija de 448 kHz. Su principal efecto es la bioestimulación celular profunda, logrando beneficios tanto a nivel terapéutico y de fisioterapia. Acelera el proceso de recuperación muscular. Carlitos no tenía la maquina en el torneo y le dio a Granollers las llaves de su habitación en el hotel The Plaza, pegado a Central Park y que se hizo famoso por la película 'Home Alone' ('Solo en Casa). El doblista se desplazó a la residencia del campeón de siete grandes, pegada a Central Park, y estuvo un buen rato tratándose mientras Alcaraz estaba ya en la pista disputando su partido con Shelton. Marcel pudo salir ayer gracias al tratamiento a jugar los cuartos de dobles ffente a Rajeev Ram y Joe Salisbury. Perdieron pero el gesto de Alcaraz ahí queda.

articles.title: Sha’Carri Richardson name-dropped during Coco Gauff’s US Open match after stunning chase-down and recovery
articles.summary: International Sports News: Sha’Carri Richardson was not on the tennis court at the US Open, but her name still came up during Coco Gauff’s match against Paula Badosa. The Olympi.
articles.body: Sha’Carri Richardson was not on the tennis court at the US Open, but her name still came up during Coco Gauff’s match against Paula Badosa. The Olympic champion and sprint star was mentioned by commentators after Gauff chased down a difficult ball with remarkable speed. Gauff had been pushed outside the court, yet she recovered quickly and reached a precise drop shot. Her movement was so quick that the broadcast team compared her to Richardson, one of the most recognizable names in track and field. The comparison caught the attention of fans watching the match.Coco Gauff’s speed brings Sha’Carri Richardson into the conversationThe moment came during a difficult point when Gauff was forced far away from the court. Instead of giving up, the American quickly changed direction and moved forward to reach Badosa’s drop shot.The commentators pointed out just how much speed Gauff needed to keep the rally alive. “You’ve got to hit the perfect drop shot against someone who moves like Sha’Carri Richardson,” one commentator said.The comparison made sense because of the way Gauff covered the court. She did not just reach the ball. She recovered from a difficult position and turned the defensive play into a chance to attack.A clip of the moment was shared on X by @greenmachine2_0. The user wrote, “Sha’carri name dropped at the U.S. Open… Her impact can’t be denied!”For Richardson, the mention was another sign that her name is now familiar well beyond track and field. She has become closely linked with speed and explosive movement, making her an easy comparison when another athlete shows those qualities.Coco Gauff and Sha’Carri Richardson have supported each otherThe connection between Gauff and Richardson also goes beyond the commentators’ comparison. The two American stars have publicly supported each other after major wins.After Gauff won the 2023 US Open for her first Grand Slam title, Richardson celebrated the achievement on Instagram. She shared the message, “Shine Lovely Shine.”Richardson also reacted to Gauff’s French Open victory last year. On her Instagram Story, she posted, “@cocogauff amazing🥹😍.”Gauff has also shown her support for Richardson. The tennis star has spoken about being inspired by the track athlete and celebrated Richardson’s Olympic success.Gauff’s own family also has a strong sports background. Her father played college basketball, while her mother competed as a track heptathlete. That athletic background has been part of Gauff’s development and is visible in the way she moves around the court.The Richardson comparison also highlights how important movement has become in modern tennis. Players need more than a powerful serve or accurate shots. They must be able to react quickly, change direction and recover from difficult positions.During Gauff’s match with Badosa, her speed was the main reason Richardson’s name came up. The moment gave track fans a reason to celebrate Richardson’s influence while showing how her reputation for speed now reaches beyond her own sport.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: US Open: Is men's singles victory a formality for Alexander Zverev or will Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe or Karen Khachanov trouble him?
articles.summary: Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe will make history on men's semi-final day with Alexander Zverev firm favourite to win his second Grand Slam of 2026; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Shelton sent defending champion Carlos Alcaraz packing in the early ‌hours of Wednesday with the pair slugging it out in the latest-finishing match in tournament history as he reached his third major semi-final, having made the final four in the 2023 US Open and 2025 Australian Open.

"That was a war," said Shelton. "The most enjoyable match that I've had in my career."

Tiafoe recovered from two sets and ‌a break down to beat compatriot Alex Michelsen, reaching the semi-finals for a third time in a thrilling fightback.

The American has provided treasured memories ​for the home fans in New York, from his dragon-slaying defeat of Rafael Nadal en route to the 2022 semi-final, ​to his blockbuster win over compatriot Shelton two ‌years ago.

But the Cincinnati runner-up this year is ready to write a new chapter this time ​around, saying: "I'm just a different person in general. Those two runs (to the semi-finals) were great, ​something I will cherish forever, but I'm not that person ⁠who I was when I made ⁠one in 2022 and when I made one in '24. I'm not that person. I'm excited to see what this ‌me does," said Tiafoe.

"I have higher hopes for myself. So yeah, it's great. The tournament ‌is still going. There's a lot more tennis to be played, a lot more sets to be played, and a lot more physical things to be done. We're going to enjoy this, but we got to keep going."

Tiafoe is enjoying a career resurgence having undertaken a big lifestyle change and fitness regime towards the end of last year.

Former world No 1 Lindsay Davenport said: "If you hear their stories about last fall, and what a dark place Frances was in, he was willing to turn over, to try and give it his best shot.

"It's not easy sometimes for players or people to do that, but he has kind of shifted everything in his life to revolve around tennis.

"Now to watch him be able to go out there and compete from two sets down, like the old Frances doesn't necessarily (do), to stick his heels in and be like 'I'm not going anywhere' - I mean, he's fighting."

While the men's draw has fallen to pieces in the absence of Jannik Sinner and with Novak Djokovic and Alcaraz falling by the wayside, Alexander Zverev has been quietly going about his business.

Luciano Darderi, the 21st seed, is the highest-ranked player Zverev has faced, while he eased past world No 70 Botic van de Zandschulp in straight sets .

The 29-year-old is a big favourite to beat unseeded Russian Karen Khachanov in the opening semi-final on Friday from 8pm on Sky Sports Tennis .

Zverev has beaten Shelton in all five of their career meetings and has lost just one of his 10 matches against Tiafoe.

Having won his first Grand Slam title at this year's French Open and then reached the Wimbledon final, the world No 2 should be feeling at home in the latter stages of major tournaments.

But he said: "I think the more often that you get to that stage, the more normal it becomes, which is something that you should never take for granted.

"I know it can change in a heartbeat in tennis. I think confidence is something that is incredibly important, but also can go away quite quickly.

"I found that out after Wimbledon where I didn't play well throughout the two tournaments on the hard courts, and then I found it again here.

"But yeah, of course I'm happy with how things are going, but looking forward, I still hope to play two good matches here."

Khachanov is seeking his first major final having reached the semi-finals of the US Open in 2022 and the Australian Open in 2023.

Khachanov was unseeded in a Grand Slam tournament for the first time since 2018 after a strange season.

He reached at least the third round of all four majors for the first time but is just 10-15 in other events, with losses in the opening rounds of all three hard-court events before coming to New York.

Zverev and Khachanov, both in the 1990s generation, have met nine times, with ​the German holding a 6-3 edge.

Their most notable encounter came in the 2021 Tokyo Olympics final, when ⁠Zverev won in straight sets to take gold, while their only previous Grand Slam meeting came at the French Open in 2018, when Zverev fought back from a set down to win in five.

articles.title: Taylor Fritz Criticizes Difference Between Official US Open Tennis Balls and Those Sold at Retail
articles.summary: Taylor Fritz believes the tennis balls used at the US Open and the ones sold at retail aren't the same.
articles.body:
Taylor Fritz believes the tennis balls used at the US Open and the ones sold at retail aren't the same.

The American star, who was upset in the fourth round by Francisco Cerúndolo, made a lengthy social media post on Thursday criticizing the difference between the balls.

He said the Wilson US Open balls he's been practicing with since being eliminated feel different than the ones used at the Washington Open, the Cincinnati Open and the US Open.

"They are sold, marketed, and labeled as the same balls, but the way they come off my racket and feel couldn't be more different," he wrote. "After that many weeks using the tournament balls, I know exactly how they respond. The balls I'm practicing with feel like literal green-dot kids' balls: incredibly soft, dead, and going nowhere."

While Fritz said he noticed a difference between the balls, he added that he wasn't using it as an excuse for his loss in New York last week.

"They were good balls, and I have no complaints about what we played with at those tournaments this summer," he said.

The point of his post wasn't to complain about the balls themselves, but rather to point out that there shouldn't be a noticeable discrepancy between the balls trained with versus the ones used in tournaments.

"That leads to the obvious the bigger issue and the reason for the rant: we need to be able to train with the same balls we compete with, and in the past I feel like this wasn't usually an issue," Fritz wrote.

Fritz also noted that he's spoken to other players since his US Open exit, and they feel the same way.

Whether the US Open or the UTSA will address Fritz's concerns remains to be seen, but he's a big name in the sport and seemingly has other players in agreement with him.

"It's disappointing that this has started to feel normal," he said. "Training is a lot less enjoyable, and a lot less productive, when you're spending it practicing with balls that are so different from what you'll use when it matters."

articles.title: US Open chief Craig Tiley tells Sky Sports Tennis he plans on keeping day and night format at Flushing Meadows in 2027
articles.summary: US Open chief Craig Tiley vows to keep same day and night format despite Ben Shelton beating Carlos Alcaraz at 3:33am local time; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Tiley, who took the helm as new CEO of USTA earlier this year after leading Tennis Australia since 2013, says he has no plans for any changes to the schedule.

It comes after Ben Shelton's five-set thriller against Carlos Alcaraz in the quarter-finals ended at 3:33am local time on Wednesday, leaving few people awake to see the near five-hour marathon reach its finale on one of the sport's biggest stages.

Players have long loved the electricity of playing night matches under the lights in the nation's biggest city.

But the tournament had already set a record with three post-2am finishes over the first six days, as well as having two other matches go past 1am.

The issue ​has gained added resonance amid a broader push by top players for increased prize money and reforms on welfare ‌and working conditions, with late finishes emerging as a flashpoint in the debate over life on the tour.

Like the US Open, the Australian Open has faced criticism for notoriously late ​finishes but the other two Grand Slams have imposed checks, with Wimbledon halting play under an 11pm local curfew and the French Open limiting night sessions to one match.

Yet a solution such as starting evening sessions earlier than 7pm is complicated by the argument that ​tennis-mad New Yorkers need time to get to Flushing Meadows after work and organisers having to manage day-and night-session ⁠crowds.

Tiley said: "I hear from a lot of people that it finishes too late and then I say, okay, and your suggestion is? I don't get anything.

"You can't control the length of the match. What's really interesting is in the last 10 years the amount of tennis from when you hit a point to when a point stops has been about the same.

"But the length of the matches on the men's side has increased by an average of about 25 minutes. That's because we now have the shot clock so everyone is taking their time, and we have the towels here which takes a bit more time and so the whole length of it is a bit longer. Not that much longer, but in fact the average time of the men's matches today is still not in the top four average times in the last 10 years.

"While it feels really late, the reality is you've got to go and look at the data, But that being said, no one wants to finish at 3.30am in the morning, although the rest of the world in the daytime saw a pretty amazing match."

"We really like the two days and two nights. Two full sessions and you get a women's match and a great men's match, and that's what our fans are telling us. They can come out and see three, four, five hours of entertainment and if it goes really long like the other night, that's a great sporting ticket so I will keep it," Tiley added.

Just hours after the Shelton-Alcaraz match concluded, the US Open took to social media with a light-hearted nod to the late night, offering a fill-in-the-blank letter for fans to ask their bosses to be excused from work on Wednesday.

"We understand how important showing up is, but sometimes you have to make time for things you're passionate about," the post on X stated. "Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton put on an absolute stellar performance during their US Open quarterfinal, and ______ was a fully committed fan who was completely locked in from start to finish."

Another suggestion that surfaces whenever late finishes dominate the conversation is reducing men's matches to best-of-three sets in the earlier rounds, though the idea is contentious among those who view five-set ⁠matches as central to Grand Slams.

"I think for the men's we should stick ​with three out of five," Frances Tiafoe said.

"I don't know where the conversation is going, what people ​are leaning to. Everyone is going to have an opinion, everyone is different.

"We've seen so many epics in five-setters. Do I love five-setters? Absolutely not. There's a lot of times where I'm up two sets to ‌love and I'd love to shake hands and go ​home. But it's tennis, man."

articles.title: Del Potro y un rival para un último partido: "Me gustaría jugar con Carlitos"
articles.standfirst: El argentino, campeón del US Open 2009, es el último jugador no nacido en Europa que ganó un grande
articles.summary: El argentino, campeón del US Open 2009, es el último jugador no nacido en Europa que ganó un grande
articles.body: Juan Martín Del Potro, a sus 37 años, sigue siendo el último campeón de Grand Slam que no nació en Europa. El argentino se impuso a Roger Federer en la final del US Open 2009. Ahora ha vuelto a Nueva York como comentarista de ESPN Latinoamérica. 'Delpo' habla con cuatro medios, entre ellos MARCA, sobre toda la actualidad del tenis,, el regreso de Alcaraz tras su lesión, la dominación con Sinner.... Pregunta. ¿Qué tal estos días en Nueva York? Respuesta. Contento de estar aquí rodeado de la nueva generación de jugadores. Ahora mi trabajo es totalmente diferente en mi día a día. Me estrené como comentarista y es un nuevo reto en mi vida. Es especial haber empezado precisamente aquí en el US Open. Espero hacerlo bien. P. ¿Cuándo fue la última vez que había estado aquí? R. El año pasado, jugué la exhibición de leyendas antes del torneo. Es un placer volver a Nueva York. Siempre que me invitan a un sitio me gusta ir porque nos tratan muy bien. Aquí me tratan como el campeón que fui y me siento muy bien. P. ¿Cómo está de salud? ¿Se puede mover sin problemas después de las lesiones que tuve en la rodilla? R. Me muevo bien porque no hago muchas cosas. He dejado de jugar a tenis. Tampoco es que vaya mucho al gimnasio. Es la única manera que tenía de no sentir dolor todos los días. Antes, para estar en exhibiciones o en clínics, necesitaba infiltrarme o tomar antiinflamatorios y tuve que parar porque no era nada nuevo para mí. Tal y como estoy ahora, puedo disfrutar de la vida. P. ¿juega a pádel? R. No, porque el pádel es aún peor que el tenis para mi rodilla. A veces voy a jugar en Argentina con amigos, pero porque son muy malos y por eso puedo jugar. Son deportes demasiado agresivos. P. ¿Cómo hace para mantenerse en forma? R. Intento comer mejor para no ganar peso. Trabajo con mi psicólogo porque es frustrante estar aquí y no poder jugar. Estoy en el proceso de encontrar una nueva vida haciendo algo que me guste. P. Hay muchos percances físicos en el tenis. Alcaraz, lesionado cuatro meses. Ahora Sinner y Fonseca. ¿Es una situación que le preocupa de cara al futuro? R. El tenis es el deporte más agresivo que existe, con el añadido de que se juegan torneos casi cada semana. Y los resultados se ven con Carlitos parado, Sinner también. Lo que pasa es que los dos son tan buenos que pueden parar cinco o seis meses y no pierden ranking ni muchos puntos. Escuché el otro día que Alcaraz dijo que va a jugar los torneos que le apetezca. Creo que es una decisión inteligente y que deberían seguir otros jugadores. P. ¿Le preocupa la situación de los torneos en Sudamérica, sobre todo con el protagonismo y el músculo económico de los eventos en el Gofo Pérsico? R. No me preocupa porque el tenis en Sudamérica tiene algo único y es la pasión por el deporte. Además, ahora tenemos a Fonseca que está empujando. Hay muchos países apostando por el tenis en otros lados, pero la pasión de nuestros aficionados nadie la va a matar. P. Usted coincidió con Carlos Alcaraz en la final del Mundial de fútbol y hablaron de su muñeca y le recomendó que no la tocara. ¿,Me puede recordar cómo fue la conversación? R. La gran diferencia es que, en mi época, cuando me lesioné la muñeca, perderme uno o dos torneos me costaba del cuatro del ranking al ocho o el diez. Ahora, con Sinner y Alcaraz por encima del resto, es muy importante que escuchen su físico. Carlitos hizo muy bien en parar cuatro o cinco meses. Cuando me lo crucé le pregunté por el tratamiento y me dijo que era conservador. Yo le dije que siguiera por ese camino y que no se tocara la muñeca. Mi error fue no querer parar porque en todos los torneos peleaba por el número cuatro, tres, dos, un Grand Slam. Sabía que si una lesión me quitaba de los torneos, como finalmente me pasó, no conseguía agarrar más ese tren. Creo que Carlitos ha tenido una buena decisión y se vio que le respondió su muñeca. Hablé con él y estaba contento. Salió de la pista sonriendo después de un partidazo con Shelton. Ben no sé si vuelve a jugar así durante cinco horas. P. Si hubiera parado como dive, ¿cree que no hubiera tenido esas cuatro cirugías en la muñeca? R. Yo creo que lo que hice era lo que tenía que hacer. Si elegía un tratamiento conservador, perdía mucho ranking. Hoy, con mi película terminada, es una película especial por todas las decisiones que tomé a lo largo de mi carrera. Los equipos médicos te asesoran , te dice hacer esto o lo otro. Para mí, en los momentos en los que me infiltraba la muñeca, era porque iba a los Grand Slam y estaba en semifinales, cuartos... Mi ranking siempre fue top10 y no quería perder eso porque nadie te garantiza si vas a regresar a ese lugar. P. Hace 17 años que Europa copa todos los títulos de Grand Slam. ¿Se puede romper esa racha este domingo en el US Open? R. Ha pasado porque el Big Three era algo especial. Nunca vamos a tener nada igual. Pero el tenis americano tiene el potencial para acabar con esa dominación. También hay jugadores argentinos, está Fonseca, que tiene mucho potencial... Creo sinceramente que tanto Shelton como Tiafoe pueden ganar aquí. No es fácil cuando vienes de estructuras que tienen menos posibilidades económicas que los grandes países sí tienen. Hay que trabajar más. No tenemos el dinero ni la infraestructura, pero sí la pasión, el amor y el corazón para trabajar duro. P. Usted tiene una relación muy cercana con Novak Djokovic. ¿Cómo ve el final de su carrera que se acerca? R. Está experimentando coas que antes nunca había sufrido, como sentirse cansado en la pista. No poder hacer el mismo daño con su tenis. Yo me lo tomo como una oportunidad de seguir viéndole jugar. A mí me da igual que gane o pierde. Es el hecho de poder verle. Es una situación parecida con Messi. Son dos granes que van a dejarlo pronto y hay que disfrutar de ellos porque el día que se vayan los vamos a llorar. Vamos a buscar un remplazo y será difícil encontrarlo. P. ¿Qué jugadores actuales le recuerdan a usted en la maneta de jugar? R. Voy a decir Sebastian Korda o Rafa Jódar. Me gustan este tipo de jugadores que son altos y que le pegan duro desde el fondo. Con un buen saque, una buena derecha y revés. También están teniendo algún que otro problema físico como me pasó a mí en su día. Les veo a los dos con mucho potencial para estar arriba en un futuro cercano. P. Si un jugador 'top' se acerca y le pide que le entrene, ¿qué le va a contestar? R. Ya han venido a pedirme, pero no era el momento. Durante la carrera, sufrimos mucho el tiempo que estamos fuera de casa, los aviones, los viajes... Si te conviertes en entrenador, vuelves a esa rutina y no estoy preparado. He tenido ofertas de los 'top' pero no es el momento. Ahora mi momento es ser comentarista. Lo estoy experimentando y me está gustando mucho. P. Si tuviera que jugar un último partido, ¿a quién elegiría, Alcaraz o Sinner? R. Yo elegiría a Carlitos porque tengo una relación más cercana con él. A Jannik le veo unas condiciones tenísticas y físicas muy paecidas a Djokovic. Son muy rápidos desde el fondo, pueden resbalar sin problemas en todas las superficies. juegan de manea muy inteligente... Pero Alcaraz tiene algo especial. Tiene una conexión increíble con el público, parece que tenga sangre de latinoamérica. Me encantaría jjugar una exhibición con él y le pediría que me dejara ganar.
