articles.title: Qinwen Zheng’s new ranking confirmed after her resurgent US Open run comes to an end
articles.summary: Qinwen Zheng’s incredible US Open run has now come to an end. Zheng underwent elbow surgery last year and had since struggled to rediscover the...
articles.body:
Qinwen Zheng's incredible US Open run has now come to an end.

Zheng underwent elbow surgery last year and had since struggled to rediscover the form that helped her reach world number four in the WTA rankings, an Australian Open final and win Olympic gold.

As a result, Zheng had dropped down the rankings and had to play qualifying at the US Open as the world number 121.

Not only did Zheng come through qualifying, but she made it all the way to the quarter-finals and she will now be rewarded in the WTA rankings.

Qinwen Zheng will climb 69 places in the WTA rankings after US Open run

Zheng beat the likes of Iga Swiatek and Madison Keys en route to the US Open quarter-finals, miraculously coming from 5-0 down in sets during both of these matches.

The 23-year-old also won the first set of her quarter-final, but Zheng was ultimately beaten 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 by Elena Rybakina, who has now become world number one as a result of this win.

Zheng will now be heavily rewarded in the WTA rankings, as she gains 470 points for winning seven matches in New York.

This means that Zheng will climb 69 places in the rankings, as she is now back in the top 60 at world number 52.

Although this is still some way from her career-high, Zheng is now starting to make strides back to her previous best.

What is next for Qinwen Zheng after the US Open?

Zheng will now have a lot of attention on her after the US Open, as she looks to continue the momentum she found in New York.

This form has come at a good time for Zheng, with the Asian swing following the US Open.

Zheng may now be ranked high enough to get into many of these tournaments, but her resurgence has come after the cut-off for the China Open .

However, with Zheng being a Chinese player, it means that she is likely to receive wildcards for multiple upcoming tournaments.

Zheng only has 65 points to defend until 2027, meaning that she now has a huge opportunity to keep climbing up the rankings in the coming weeks.

articles.title: US Open women's semifinals: Score, live updates as Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula open the evening, followed by Coco Gauff vs. Elena Rybakina
articles.summary: The 2026 US Open women's semifinals will feature each of the tournament's top-four seeded competitors.
articles.body: Tennis fans will get a treat in the US Open women's semifinals, featuring each of the tournament's top-four seeds looking to further their quest to take home the title at Flushing Meadows.No. 3 Jessica Pegula will face the tournament's No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka in a rematch of the 2024 US Open final, where Sabalenka took home her first title in the tournament, defeating Pegula in two sets, 7-5, 7-5. articles.body:
Coco Gauff's pursuit of a second US Open title came to an end on Thursday.

Elena Rybakina defeated the 23-year-old American, snapping her 11-match win streak.

In the other semifinal, Aryna Sabalenka defeated Jessica Pegula, keeping her quest for an elusive three-peat at the US Open alive.

We have everything you need below, from results to takeaways.

No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka def. No. 3 Jessica Pegula, 7-5, 6-2

No. 2 Elena Rybakina def. No. 4 Coco Gauff, 3-6, 6-4, 6-4

Elena Rybakina defeated Coco Gauff in a thrilling three-set match, extending her remarkable 2026 season.

Gauff frustrated Rybakina early with her strong defense, forcing the No. 2 seed into 18 unforced errors in the opening set.

However, in the second set, Rybakina found her rhythm, placing her serves with precision and breaking Gauff's momentum.

Although Gauff responded, Rybakina broke again, sending the match into a decisive third set.

In the final set, Rybakina continued to hold serve comfortably as Gauff's forehand began to falter.

Serving down 3-2, Gauff faced a love-30 deficit but managed to save both break points and held serve after a nearly seven-minute game.

Rybakina maintained the pressure and ultimately secured a crucial break to take a 5-3 lead.

Although Gauff broke back to momentarily shift the momentum, Rybakina immediately countered with a break to seal the victory.

Meanwhile, Aryna Sabalenka is now just one win away from becoming the third woman in the Open Era to claim three consecutive US Open titles.

The world No. 1 overpowered Jessica Pegula in straight sets to advance to her eighth consecutive hard-court Grand Slam final.

In the first set, both players held serve with ease until Sabalenka secured a decisive late break to win it.

In the second set, Sabalenka elevated her performance, dominating with her serve-plus-one tactic and relentlessly pressuring Pegula's second serve.

Sabalenka won 14 of 19 points on Pegula's second serve and hit 29 winners.

It's the third straight year that Sabalenka has dashed Pegula's title hopes.

articles.title: Coco Gauff bounced from US Open by new world No.1 Elena Rybakina, who will face Aryna Sabalenka in final
articles.summary: In front of a fired-up, sold-out crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium, the second of two women’s semifinals saw the No. 2 seed Rybakina defeat the No. 4 Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4.
articles.body: Just when Coco Gauff thought she was back in control of her semifinal bout with Elena Rybakina, she wasn’t. In front of a fired-up, sold-out crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium, the second of two US Open women’s semifinals saw the No. 2 seed Rybakina defeat the No. 4 seed Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4. Gauff started strong, which was no surprise as she came into Thursday on a heater – winning 11 straight matches. Behind a strong service game, the 22-year-old cruised to a 6-3 first-set win over Rybakina. With former first lady Michelle Obama looking on and a very pro-American crowd cheering for Gauff, the US star never faced a break point and only lost four points on her first serve while her opponent hit 18 unforced errors. But the Russian-born Kazakhstani showed why she will be the world’s new No. 1 come Monday with a red hot start to open the second set. After jumping out to a 4-1 lead, the American fought back, eventually tying the score at 4-4 with the crowd urging her on. However, Rybakina shook off the break, taking the next two games to force a deciding third set to determine who will join women’s top seed Aryna Sabalenka in the final. Both Gauff and Rybakina went back and forth, finding themselves deadlocked at 3-3 before the 27-year-old Rybakina started to impose her will and won the next two games to put her on the brink of her first final appearance at Flushing Meadows. Gauff did not back down, clawing back to break back and make it 5-4. She let out a primal scream as the New York crowd showed their love and support. This was the moment Gauff appeared ready to take advantage of the momentum. But Rybakina showed no intimidation, quickly coming through with a decisive break to clinch the victory after Gauff sent her overhead shot out of bounds, much to the shock of those there to root on the American. “I know you guys wanted Coco to win,” Rybakina said afterward. Rybakina will now look to win her third grand slam in her career, but gave praise to Gauff following the match. “Coco, she’s a great player. It’s always tough to play against her. Even if sometimes her first serve doesn’t go, the second one is so heavy,” Rybakina told ESPN. “… Took a deep breath. Was trying to talk positive to myself and just told myself I need to fight and try to show good tennis.” Sabalenka books another US Open final place Sabalenka advanced to her fourth straight US Open final after overwelming No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2 in Thursday’s first semifinal. The first set was not a walk in the park for the two-time reigning champion. The Belarusian star and the American traded games back and forth until the deciding game, where Sabalenka dominated Pegula’s serve to avoid a first-set tiebreak and win the opener 7-5. Sabalenka quickly went up 4-1 in the second set before Pegula battled to take the sixth game. But frustration boiled over for Pegula after dropping the next game, which resulted in her throwing her racket to the ground. Sabalenka clinched another title chance this weekend with a strong forehand that Pegula failed to connect with. She has now won 19 straight matches at the US Open. The 28-year-old won this tournament in 2024 and 2025 after losing to Coco Gauff in the 2023 championship match. She can become the third-ever woman to win three straight in the open era, joining Serena Williams and Chris Evert. Afterward, Sabalenka said she had “no complaints” about how the match went. “Last time I played Jessica, it was almost impossible to get the win, so I am super happy to play such tennis in front of you all,” Sabalenka addressed the crowd while speaking to ESPN. “Thank you for the atmosphere, and honestly guys, you are the best. Your respect to me is priceless and I know you wanted (Pegula) to win but thank you for being so respectful to me.” Sabalenka once again rocked some custom jewelry during the match that has people talking. She previously said her vintage-looking Material Good necklace looks heavy, but it isn’t. “It’s very chic, bright and light,” she said. Rybakina and Sabalenka know each other’s games well, having previously met 17 times on the WTA Tour, with Rybakina winning the last two tilts – earning the Australian Open and WTA Finals titles. Sabalenka has won the two most recent meet-ups – the championship match at Indian Wells and in the Miami Open semis en route to winning the title (over Gauff). The women’s final is scheduled for Saturday at 4 p.m. ET. This story has been updated with additional reporting.

But once Sabalenka found her opening, the match changed dramatically. She began attacking Pegula's second serve with greater aggression and carried that momentum into a dominant second set, producing some of her best tennis of the tournament.“No complaints,” Sabalenka said. “I’m just super happy that I was able to pull out such tennis.”The Belarusian will play either No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina or No. 4 Coco Gauff in Saturday's final. A victory would make Sabalenka the first player since Serena Williams in 2012-14 to win three consecutive U.S. Open titles.Sabalenka is also set to surrender the No. 1 ranking to Rybakina next week, ending her run of 99 consecutive weeks at the top. But she has made it clear that another trophy in New York would make giving up the ranking far easier to accept.And based on the way she dismantled Pegula, Sabalenka will enter Saturday's final with plenty of belief.Sabalenka turns a tight contest into a one-sided finishThe semifinal initially followed the pattern of Sabalenka's previous two meetings with Pegula at the business end of the U.S. Open. She has not lost at Flushing Meadows since Gauff defeated her in the 2023 final.The result also maintained the dominance of the tournament's top four seeds. For the first time since 1975, all four women's semifinalists came from the top four positions in the draw.Sabalenka, Rybakina and Gauff have already collected multiple major titles, while Pegula continues to chase the first Grand Slam trophy of her career.Pegula hangs on before Sabalenka finds the breakthroughPegula, a Buffalo, New York native, had hoped her strongest surface and favourite Grand Slam would finally provide the setting for a maiden major title.She managed to stay with Sabalenka early on. But that was where Sabalenka finally broke the deadlock.A backhand winner gave her the first opening. Pegula then pushed a forehand long before Sabalenka produced another winner to earn set point. She closed out the set two points later, turning a finely balanced contest on its head.The hard courts that suit Pegula also happen to provide the perfect stage for Sabalenka's power game, and the Belarusian began making that difference count.Pegula has no answer as Sabalenka takes controlSabalenka struck again in Pegula's second service game of the second set. She eventually pounced on a 77 mph second serve, driving a forehand back at 90 mph. Pegula could not recover in time, and Sabalenka moved ahead 3-1.It was exactly the kind of pressure Sabalenka had said she enjoyed facing against Pegula.The American entered the semifinal having recorded the most wins on tour this season, while also sharing the lead for hard-court victories. Sabalenka had described her as the kind of opponent who could test her and force her to respond whenever she was put under pressure.On Thursday, Sabalenka supplied those answers repeatedly.Pegula's frustration boiled over late in the match. articles.summary: Soon-to-be world number one Elena Rybakina will face Aryna Sabalenka in a blockbuster US Open final between the tournament's top two seeds.
articles.body:
Soon-to-be world number one Elena Rybakina produced a gritty comeback against Coco Gauff to reach the US Open final, in which she will face Aryna Sabalenka in a blockbuster showdown between the tournament's top two seeds.

Rybakina is guaranteed to end Sabalenka's 99-week reign as world number one and will replace the Belarusian at the top when the rankings are updated on Monday.

But the Kazakh second seed could rub more salt in Sabalenka's wounds if she can deny the top seed a third successive US Open title in Saturday's showpiece.

Sabalenka sent a warning to her rivals as she overpowered home hope Jessica Pegula 7-5 6-2 to keep alive her bid to become the third woman in the Open era to win the New York singles title three times in a row.

Rybakina will stand in her way after she fought back to beat American fourth seed Gauff 3-6 6-4 6-4 and silence the partisan crowd.

"I took a deep breath and just told myself I needed to fight and show good tennis," Rybakina said.

The 27-year-old is chasing her third Grand Slam title after winning Wimbledon in 2022 and beating Sabalenka in January's Australian Open final.

It will be the first time the top two women's seeds have contested a US Open final since Serena Williams beat Victoria Azarenka in the 2013 showpiece.

'I was super desperate' - Sabalenka's 'best match this year'

Sabalenka has not been beaten in New York since losing the 2023 final to Gauff, but there were doubts over her title defence following a poor run-up to the tournament.

After a strong start to the season and winning the 'Sunshine Double' at Indian Wells and Miami in March, Sabalenka suffered a quarter-final defeat at Roland Garros and a fourth-round exit at Wimbledon.

However, she has found her form again, dropping just one set en route to the final.

"I was super desperate," Sabalenka said after her win over Pegula.

"It feels for me, talking about Grand Slams, like a last push of the season.

"I wanted it badly to go to the finals, and of course, I want to go all the way."

In a tense opening set, Sabalenka bristled with frustration early on as unforced errors crept into her game while Pegula settled quickly and struck the ball cleanly.

But eventually the four-time major singles winner found her rhythm and, after striking decisively at 6-5 to take the first set, she cranked up the power.

Pegula looked helpless as Sabalenka raced through the second set, with the Belarusian pounding 29 winners to her 12.

The victory meant Sabalenka broke the Open era record for the most Grand Slam hard-court finals in a row, with the 28-year-old reaching every major final on her favoured surface since the 2023 Australian Open.

For 32-year-old Pegula - the only semi-finalist without a Grand Slam title - it is yet another US Open defeat by long-time rival Sabalenka.

Sabalenka denied the third seed a maiden major in the 2024 final, while she also got the better of her in last year's semi-finals - although Pegula had won their most recent meeting in June's Berlin Open.

"I do think she probably would have beaten 99% of people," Pegula said.

"Probably the best match she's played this year."

Harrison & GB's Skupski into men's doubles final

Hewett & Reid into men's wheelchair doubles final

Listen: US Open - tennis remembers 9/11 25 years on

Rybakina earns chance to back up new number one status

Rybakina's ascent to the top of the world rankings is already assured but she has made it clear that for all the prestige of being number one, winning titles is what she really cares about.

"It's just a number right now, my goal is to win the tournaments which I play," the 27-year-old said before her semi-final.

A three-set victory over Gauff showed all of Rybakina's resilience and ability to absorb a setback - coming from a set down and then being broken when serving for the match - before striking back.

But for much of the match, she was well short of her destructive best.

"I definitely need to step my game up [in the final], serve better than today, stay aggressive and really go for my shots," the two-time major winner added.

The prospect of a final between the top two seeds is tantalising enough but that it is the outgoing number one taking on her successor makes it all the more mouth-watering.

While Sabalenka holds the edge in the head-to-head with 10 wins in 17 meetings, including beating Rybakina in the semi-finals in Miami and the final at Indian Wells this year, the Kazakh came out on top when they met in January's Australian Open final.

Sabalenka led 3-0 in the deciding set in Melbourne but eventually fell to a third defeat in her past four Grand Slam finals.

Meanwhile, Rybakina's only loss in three previous major finals was to Sabalenka in Australia in 2023.

Coco Gauff fell short in her bid to play for a second U.S. Open title Thursday night in Queens.

Gauff won her first set of the semifinal before Elena Rybakina came back to claim a 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 victory.

Gauff dominated Thursday's first set in front of an appreciative crowd at Arthur Ashe.

Rybakina took an early lead in the second set before Gauff came back to even the score at 4-4.

After Rybakina earned two break points, Gauff put a forehand into the net to send the game to a deciding third set.

Gauff again evened the third set at 3-3 but was unable to complete her comeback before Rybakina closed out the win.

Gauff became the first American teen to win the U.S. Open when she defeated Sabalenka in the 2023 final.

She was eliminated from the 2024 and 2025 tournaments in the Round of 16, then made it back to the semis in 2026 following a comeback quarterfinal win over Mirra Andreeva.

Rybakina battled back to upset home favourite Gauff 3-6 6-4 6-4 in a fierce semi-final showdown to secure a ​title showdown with defending champion Aryna Sabalenka and stay ​on course for a ‌third Grand Slam crown.

"Of course there were nerves," admitted Rybakina in her on-court interview. "Coco is a great player. It's always tough to play her. Even if sometimes her first serve doesn't go the second one is so heavy it's difficult to dictate the rallies. I took a deep breath, tried to talk positive with myself and just told myself I need to fight and try to show good tennis."

Gauff absorbed relentless pressure ​but stayed strong to draw errors from the Kazakh, ​breaking in the sixth ⁠game and taking the ⁠opening set in front of a passionate crowd ‌that included former first lady Michelle Obama.

Rybakina capitalised on some sloppy play ‌by the fourth-seeded American in the second set to level the match.

Rybakina, the Australian Open champion, gained control ​with her power and broke ​to go 5-3 ahead in ​the decider. Gauff hit back ⁠with a break of her own but her comeback bid faltered ⁠when she could not ​hold serve, as Rybakina broke ​to close out the win.

Gauff said: "Right now, it sucks. My dad said 'you accomplished so many great things this summer'. I was like I don't care about the summer. So right now that's where my head is at."

Sabalenka keeps bid for three-peat alive

Top seed Sabalenka relied on her usual power to chip away at ​Pegula, sending over ⁠29 winners and ⁠seven aces before closing it out with ‌an unreturnable shot deep in the American's territory.

Third-seeded ‌Pegula, runner-up in 2024, started the match with a poised performance but eventually succumbed to ⁠the Belarusian's power, as ​a bevy of costly ​mistakes in the ​second set undermined her best ⁠efforts.

"I ​was so desperate for the win, I wanted ⁠it badly," said Sabalenka.

Pegula got off to a near-pristine start, saving an early break point with a fine forehand winner, ‌as Sabalenka struggled to rein in her frustrations, whacking her racket on the court after a double fault in the ninth game.

Pegula held her serve in ⁠the 10th, but the defending champion soon hit her stride as she ​broke her opponent from the baseline on set point.

She ​used her best weapon to her advantage again to go ​up 3-1 in the second set, firing off a forehand ⁠winner from the baseline on break point, as Pegula struggled to find her early polish before Sabalenka broke her again on match point.

"I can say that I feel confident and I feel mentally and physically really strong right now," ⁠said Sabalenka, who earned the respect of ​the partisan fans at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Pegula, 32, is still looking for a maiden Grand Slam title and admitted she faced an almost impossible task with Sabalenka in that mood.

She said: "I don't know who p****d her off today - hopefully it wasn't me totally, but it might have been - I don't know. She played insane. She played a super-high level.

"Honestly, I don't really know if there was much I could do today."

articles.body:
The family home of the celebrated architect behind the Lloyd's building and the Pompidou Centre has been donated to the National Trust.

Richard Rogers' home in Wimbledon, south-west London, known as the Rogers House, was built in 1968 and has become a landmark in its own right.

The property, 22 Parkside, was designed by Rogers and his first wife Su Rogers, also an architect. Lord Rogers died in 2021 aged 88 .

The National Trust has said the "extraordinary gift" will "protect one of the UK's most important examples of modern architecture for future generations".

The home was built by the couple for Richard's parents, Nino and Dada Rogers.

Ben Rogers, the son of Richard and Su - who divorced in the early 1970s - said: "Twenty-two Parkside is much more than a family home.

"It is one of the most important buildings my father and mother created – a place where many of the ideas that would go on to influence my father's work and some of the world's most celebrated architecture were first tested and explored.

"As a family, we wanted to ensure that this remarkable house would be protected, cared for and shared with future generations, rather than remaining a private asset.

"The National Trust brings the expertise, public purpose and long-term commitment needed to safeguard its future, while opening up its story to students, researchers and visitors."

Ruthie Rogers, who was married to the celebrated architect from 1973 until his death five years ago, said her late husband "regarded public access to culture – whether architecture, art, theatre, music, or design – as one of the great aspirations in life".

She said: "It filled him with such joy that the public would have access to this house that was once private, a house that was a prototype for what he thought houses could be for all."

National Trust director-general Hilary McGrady said: "We are profoundly grateful to the Rogers family for placing this extraordinary house in our care.

"Their generosity means that 22 Parkside will now become part of our shared inheritance, belonging not to a single family but to the people of England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

"This extraordinary gift will ensure that a building where world-changing ideas were born continues to inspire new generations of thinkers, makers and creators."

The charity plans to host guided visits, educational partnerships and interactive, digital content at the house, with the aim it "becomes a creative and educational resource for schools, universities and other heritage organisations around the world".

articles.title: 9/11 anniversary: US Open commemorates 25-year anniversary of attack on city
articles.summary: On Friday, the US Open will pause and remember the victims of the 9/11 terror attack that took place 25 years ago.
articles.body:
The Arthur Ashe Stadium will glow light blue from dusk until dawn as the US Open marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

American flags will be flown at half-mast as New York remembers the 2,977 people who died when hijackers crashed passenger jets into the Twin Towers in Manhattan on that day in 2001.

That year's US Open had concluded just two days earlier, with Lleyton Hewitt winning the men's singles title.

American player James Blake had lost in the second round that year and was in Augusta, Georgia, on Tuesday, 11 September.

But the New York-born future world number four says the day "shattered the guise of safety" felt by Americans and many professional tennis players.

"It was something that I just couldn't believe could happen in the States," Blake told BBC Sport.

"I don't know if we were all naive, or living under the guise of safety and feeling that everything was going to be OK, but it kind of shattered that for a while.

"There was a lot of panic, at every level - whether it be from the highest of highs in the political world to the people on the ground, to everyone around Ground Zero."

US Open: Tennis remembers 9/11, 25 years on

Blake, who would later reach two US Open quarter-finals, was in Augusta for a sweat test, having struggled with cramp during the tournament.

His father, though, was still in New York, where he worked. With mobile phone networks overloaded, there was an uncomfortable wait to discover he was safe and well.

Blake was living in Florida at the time, and with planes grounded, took a hire car from Augusta back to Tampa.

His next tournament was in Hong Kong two weeks later, and he admits it was far from easy to board the plane.

"It was definitely scary because I think you get so isolated in tennis," he said.

"You feel like the little bubble you are in, where you are a kind of travelling circus, is normal.

"And then when you realise how restricted travel can be, it wakes you up a little bit to the reality and how quickly things can change.

"It felt like there was a safety net around you. We lived in a bit of a dream world where you are living your dream of playing a sport for a living, and that can all be taken away."

Many domestic sporting events were paused in the aftermath of the attacks, and the Ryder Cup - which had been due to take place at The Belfry in England later that month - was postponed by twelve months.

In Blake's view, the return of competitive sport helped enormously.

"I think that was one of the things that brought the country back," he said.

"Sports were stopped, but when they came back having [then President] George W Bush throwing out the first pitch at a Yankees game - I'm not a Yankees fan, and I can't say I was necessarily a George W Bush fan - I was almost in tears at that moment.

"It was special to have a sitting president [do that]. And it also signified we are back - we are going to have sports, we are going to continue on with our lives.

"The world seemed like it was back on track in a small way."

There is always a ceremony to mark the anniversary when the date falls during the US Open, and there will be a minute's silence before both of Friday's men's singles semi-finals.

Before the night session - and the all-American semi-final between Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe - a giant flag will be unfurled on court as R&B artist JoJo sings The Star-Spangled Banner.

"To me it's a really poignant moment," Blake added.

"The 2001 US Open, I remember so well. What would have happened if it happened two or three days earlier, and we were all still there?

"To be perfectly honest, a lot of times I feel playing the national anthem at smaller sporting events is unnecessary.

"But for the US Open, being such an international event and having it around 9/11, I I think it is a great moment.

articles.title: The crowd wanted Coco Gauff but got Elena Rybakina instead
articles.summary: Don’t let them tell you the crowd doesn’t care about the tennis. At the very least, they care about tennis players. Or a tennis player. They care about Coco.
articles.body: Don’t let them tell you the crowd doesn’t care about the tennis. At the very least, they care about tennis players. Or a tennis player. They care about Coco. The crowd at the US Open women’s semifinals wanted to watch Coco Gauff – a charismatic American star with a buoyant athleticism that belies her strength and an even more buoyant affect that belies her depth – win. After Jessica Pegula fell to Aryna Sabalenka earlier in the evening, Gauff was the only American woman remaining in the tournament. But the enthusiasm for Gauff goes beyond patriotism. At Arthur Ashe, where she won her first grand slam at 19 years old back in 2023, she is beloved. The feeling is mutual. “No disrespect to other tournaments,” Gauff said after the match, “but every US Open is kind of where my mind is.” By then, she had lost, 3-6, 6-4, 6-4, to Elena Rybakina, the new No. 1 in the sport. “I enjoyed the atmosphere,” the soft-spoken Rybakina said of her first time playing on Arthur Ashe at night. “Even if the crowd mostly was for Coco.” “Co-co! Co-co!” chanted the crowd after she won the fourth game of the first set. This was when it seemed she might dominate the match. The umpire, in a role that has been regularly tasked with chastising rowdy spectators at the tournament this year, offered a bemused but pointed “Thank you…” in response. About an hour and a half later, with her time in the tournament slipping away, someone yelled “Come on, Coco!” It was a clear and piercing cheer. Supportive, but not celebratory. It didn’t feel fatalistic. Gauff was battling hard, the effort audible as she fended off Rybakina’s steady surge from behind. It was, at times, effective. When she broke the Kazakhstani star’s serve to stay alive in the final set, the crowd couldn’t help leaping to their feet. But then, as the final game unraveled, the cheers became more of a plea. “Come on, Coco!” The impressive thing about live tennis is how fast it is. Except for when it’s slow. When Rybakina sends a volley high into the air and Gauff has time to study the arc and the whole stadium gets impatient for her to just spike the damn ball, which she will as soon as it comes close enough. Or slow like the final flight of a ball that’s been ping ponged back and forth like a whiplash, except now Gauff sees or senses that Rybakina’s strength could be her downfall and lets the line drive go all the way, landing and bouncing harmlessly out of bounds. That trick of time disappears, though for the final point of the night. The game speed is back as Gauff’s last-ditch volley flies just long. Suddenly, it’s over. The impressive thing about Arthur Ashe is how big it is – a cavernous cathedral to tennis. Except when it’s strikingly intimate. They say the media seats are worse than they used to be, bumped out of the lower bowl to make room for more luxury options. But you can still see when a player’s shoulders go from coiled at the ready to released, not in relaxation but in resignation. After every point allowed, there’s a slight slump. And, actually, maybe it is a moment or a millisecond to relax – or, at least, a release, a physical unwinding of the expectations inherent in that rally. On to the next. Until there is no more. The discourse-inspiring but undeniably appealing atmosphere of the US Open is one of fanfare and decadence. The soundtrack, the swell of the collective gasps, even the lighting at night gives it the effect of building toward something big. Tennis matches feel like movie scenes, the tension shifting between easy-to-decipher binaries. It’s a blessing and curse for the sport, how quickly a casual fan can buy in and lend their energy to the ambiance. Except when the night is done and the fan favorite has just fallen to a skilled stoic. “I know you guys wanted Coco to win,” Rybakina said in her immediate post-match comments, still breathing heavily from what had been a worthy fight for a ticket to the final. She called herself lucky. But the fans she was speaking to didn’t hear it. They were already gone, having evacuated the site of collective disappointment faster than seemed possible for a crowd of such size. Gauff gathered her things as quickly as her many supporters did. And somewhere along the way between walking off Arthur Ashe and appearing before the media, her father reminded her that she’s accomplished so many great things this summer, which has been a consistent stretch of success. “I don’t care about the summer,” she told him. She cares about the US Open, about giving these fans what they came to see. “This is the tournament I want to perform at,” Gauff said. “I mean, I did perform, but the one that you want to come out with a win.”

articles.title: Un "doloroso" hematoma causado por una prueba antidopaje deja KO a una tenista: "No encontraba la vena..."
articles.standfirst: La molestias que le provoca el hematoma obligaron a Lucrezia Stefanini a retirarse del WTA 125 de Barranquilla
articles.summary: La molestias que le provoca el hematoma obligaron a Lucrezia Stefanini a retirarse del WTA 125 de Barranquilla
articles.body: Lucrezia Stefanini, la tenista que denunció amenazas de los apostadores ("me mandaron la foto de una pistola y el nombre de mis padres"), compartió en sus redes sociales el resultado de accidentado control antidopaje al que tuvo que someterse el 2 de septiembre en el US Open. La actual número 119 del ránking WTA mostró las secuelas, visibles una semana después de su eliminación ante Jasmine Paolini, que le dejó el control. La molestias que le provoca el hematoma obligaron a Lucrezia Stefanini a retirarse del WTA 125 de Barranquilla. Lucrezia Stefanini publicó unas fotografías del hematoma en el brazo, acompañada de una descripción detallada de lo sucedido. "Hace una semana, en el US Open, durante un control antidopaje, la responsable no logró encontrar la vena y, en lugar de cambiar de zona, siguió moviendo la aguja dentro de mi brazo para intentar localizarla. ¿El resultado? Este bonito hematoma que sigue aquí una semana después", compartió la tenista italiana. Lucrezia Stefanini publicó la evolución del doloroso hematoma, que le impide realizar "actividades cotidianas". "Me pregunto: ¿es normal que un control antidopaje se realice de esta manera? Y sobre todo: ¿es este el trato reservado a todas las jugadoras?", se preguntó. Stefanini confirmó que el hematoma "me duele incluso al hacer cosas cotidianas".

articles.title: US Open 2026 semi-finals: Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton look to bounce back from late-night finishes
articles.summary: New York is known as the city that never sleeps. But that comes at a price for US Open stars - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev.
articles.body:
New York is known as the city that never sleeps - and so it has been at this year's US Open.

A number of matches have started late and finished in the early hours, backing up the city's reputation as a playground for the nocturnal.

But when some players - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev - are heading to bed as Manhattan commuters are waking up for work, it raises questions about fairness.

Three of top seed Zverev's five matches over the past fortnight have finished past 1am.

"I've been to bed as late as 6:45am in the past week so I'm kind of a bit jet-lagged," Zverev said.

"I feel like I'm playing the Australian Open in New York right now."

Friday's semi-final against Karen Khachanov - not before 15:00 local time/20:00 BST - will be the first time the German has played in the day at this year's US Open.

By contrast, unseeded Khachanov has not been on court beyond midnight. He also has slightly longer to prepare after his quarter-final against Alexander Blockx finished shortly before 19:00 local time on Wednesday.

American eighth seed Shelton did not complete his last-eight victory over Carlos Alcaraz until 3:34am on Wednesday.

Shelton faces 11th seed Frances Tiafoe, who wrapped up his quarter-final about 19:00 on Tuesday after beating US compatriot Alex Michelsen in a five-set epic.

" The advantage of the opponent who has played earlier in the day will be big - they've had that full evening's rest and a good night's sleep," Matt Little, who was Andy Murray's long-time strength and conditioning coach, told BBC Sport.

"We can all relate to it - if you have one really bad night's sleep, you have the knock-on effect of that for the coming days."

Little saw the effects first hand when Murray infamously finished a match at 4am at the 2023 Australian Open, with the former world number one managing only three hours sleep before returning to Melbourne Park about 11am the following day.

Zverev did not go to bed until gone 5am following his opening three victories at Flushing Meadows and stayed up to watch Shelton beat Alcaraz on his night off.

Shelton, who meets Tiafoe in Friday's night session (19:00 local time/00:00 BST, Sat), insisted he would pull up "all right" after two days off court.

"He'll have to be napping to catch up some sleep," said Little.

"On the nutritional side, he'll be making sure he gets as many carbs and as much protein as he can in for that next match, and trying to get back to a bit of a routine.

"It's about making sure you can optimise the hydration and get as much sleep as possible without completely going into a full slumber."

Murray described the situation in Melbourne - where he beat Thanasi Kokkinakis in the second-latest finish in Grand Slam history - as a "farce".

Few disagreed, and slight tweaks have been made in an attempt to limit matches finishing at the crack of dawn.

In response to Murray's match, the Australian Open cut the number of day-session matches on the main courts from three to two to reduce the risk of night sessions being delayed.

In early 2024, the ATP and WTA created new rules which prevented tour matches - played over three sets and not five like the Slams - starting after 23:00. These rules, however, do not apply at the majors.

Last week, former world number one Venus Williams and her opponent Sofia Kenin began their first-round match at 12:13am - the latest start in US Open history.

It was one of three matches which finished post-2am in the first seven nights, with three others ending after 1am, while Shelton's victory over Alcaraz was the latest finish in US Open history.

"Something has got to give," said 18-time Grand Slam singles champion Martina Navratilova. "This is not OK and it is not normal."

Some argue these occasions are the essence of the US Open - and a raucous sporting representation of the city which never sleeps.

The volume of early-morning matches has increased at Flushing Meadows this fortnight, although Tuesday's play finishing at 3:34am on Wednesday was the product of unusual circumstances.

All three preceding quarter-finals on Arthur Ashe Stadium - Aryna Sabalenka beating Linda Noskova and Jessica Pegula overcoming Emma Navarro, with Tiafoe's win sandwiched in the middle - went the full distance.

Data shows matches are becoming longer - so what is the solution?

Starting the US Open night sessions earlier is the most common proposal.

That is met by a resistance from television executives and the practicality of New York life, with many fans unlikely to arrive at Flushing Meadows much before 7pm.

There is a more extreme suggestion - cutting back on the best-of-five sets format at the Slams.

That idea gained further traction after Andrew Abdo - Tennis Australia's recently-appointed chief executive - suggested the Australian Open could look to reduce men's matches to three sets in the future.

Abdo's comments provoked a backlash, with Tiafoe among those defending the traditional way.

"Do I love five-setters? Absolutely not," Tiafoe said.

"But it's tennis, man. I grew up watching so many incredible five-setters.

"Novak-Rafa, Federer-Rafa, epic five-setters that go on for hours and hours. That's the history of the game."

articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW YORK CITY: Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi and Ukraine’s Antonina Sushkova pulled off another upset on Thursday, shocking the fourth-seeded Russian comb.
articles.body: NEW YORK CITY: Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi and Ukraine’s Antonina Sushkova pulled off another upset on Thursday, shocking the fourth-seeded Russian combine of Felitsata Dorofeeva-Rybas and Anna Pushkareva 6-4, 6-4 in 64 minutes to reach the US Open junior girls’ doubles semi-finals.It was another clean performance from the Indo-Ukrainian duo, who had knocked out fifth seeds Jana Kovackova and Katerina Zajickova of the Czech Republic in the second round.Maaya and Sushkova, both 17, were particularly strong on serve, with the duo winning 70% of their first-serve points, 23 of 33, and saving seven of the eight break points they faced. They struck four aces and 21 winners, converting three of the six break points they earned. More importantly, they made the key points count despite trailing the Russians 58-59 in total points won.Maaya, from Coimbatore and based in Spain, has partnered different players at the two previous majors where she played doubles this year, teaming up with American Thea Frodin at Wimbledon where they made the quarterfinals and Australian Renee Alame at the Australian Open.Next up for Maaya and Sushkova are American twins Kristina and Annika Penickova. articles.title: US Open: Sky Sports agrees three-year extension to show the US Open until end of 2030
articles.summary: Sky Sports agrees three-year extension to broadcast the US Open; 2026 competition reaches thrilling conclusion at Flushing Meadows this weekend; watch Aryna Sabalenka take on Elena Rybakina in the women's final on Saturday, followed by the men's final on Sunday
articles.body:
As part of the partnership with the United States Tennis Association (USTA), Sky Sports will retain exclusive live coverage of all men's and women's singles, doubles, mixed doubles, juniors and wheelchair competitions throughout the three-week tournament. The agreement was negotiated by the USTA's media rights partner, IMG.

Alongside broadcast rights, fans in the UK and Ireland will also be able to catch up on all the action with clips and highlights available across Sky's digital and social platforms.

This year's coverage has featured augmented reality graphics, enhanced data integrations, in-depth touchscreen analysis and behind-the-scenes content, bringing fans closer to the action than ever before.

Sky's tennis coverage is led by presenter Gigi Salmon and includes expert analysis from Tim Henman and Laura Robson, alongside additional talent and co-commentators at events throughout the season. Match commentary is provided by Jonathan Overend.

The announcement comes amid a drama-filled US Open featuring the shock first-round exit of 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic and the latest finish in tournament history between Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz as the American emerged victorious at 3.33am.

A thrilling women's final meanwhile awaits as World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka takes on World No 2 Elena Rybakina on Saturday.

Jonathan Licht, Chief Executive Officer Sky Sports UK & Ireland, said : "The US Open is one of the highlights of the sporting calendar, featuring the biggest names in both the men's and women's games, all set against the spectacular New York backdrop. We're delighted to extend our partnership with the USTA, reinforcing our shared commitment to embracing innovation, showcasing the best in the sport and delivering world-class coverage for viewers. This renewal further cements Sky Sports' position as the home of sport in the UK and Ireland, offering fans unrivalled breadth and value all year round."

Kirsten Corio, Chief Commercial Officer, USTA: "The US Open and Sky Sports have been trusted partners for many years, and we're excited to continue such a strong relationship with this renewal. Sky shares our commitment to delivering innovative and cutting-edge coverage to a great audience of tennis fans in the U.K. and Ireland, and we're confident that our continued partnership will have a direct impact on tennis' extraordinary growth and deepen fans' connection with the game."

Live tennis is available all year on Sky, including full coverage of the ATP and WTA Tours on Sky Sports or available to stream with NOW and the Sky Sports app. Sky Sports will broadcast over 4,000 matches and 80 tournaments this season.

The partnership extension adds to Sky's already unrivalled portfolio in the UK and Ireland with more top-quality sport than anywhere else, with most sport rights renewed until near the end of the decade. That includes 1,500 games from the Premier League, WSL, EFL and SPFL, exclusive live coverage from every Formula 1 race weekend until the end of 2034, home men's and women's international England cricket, every shot from the golf Majors, year-round coverage of darts, world class boxing from promoters Zuffa and MVP, and more action from the NFL, Netball Super League and rugby league.

The US Open is live on Sky Sports from August 30. Stream tennis with no contract on NOW and the Sky Sports App . You can also watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports.

articles.summary: The US Open has reached its final four competitors.
articles.body:
The US Open has reached its final four competitors.

By now, it's common knowledge that no American man has captured a Grand Slam title since Andy Roddick's victory at the 2003 US Open.

However, for just the second time in the past 15 years, an American man will play in a major final.

Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe are set to face off in what will be only the third all-American men's US Open semifinal of this century.

Meanwhile, top-ranked Alexander Zverev will go head-to-head with unseeded Karen Khachanov in the other semifinal.

Read on for the ultimate predictions for tonight's matches.

Alexander Zverev steps into the semifinals, aiming for his third straight appearance in a Grand Slam final.

After being pushed to five sets in his opening two matches, Zverev has rediscovered his rhythm. His serve is clicking, and his refined forehand continues to pay dividends.

On the other side of the net, Karen Khachanov arrives as the lowest-ranked US Open semifinalist since Grigor Dimitrov made his run in 2019.

This season has not been kind to Khachanov, who has struggled to find consistency and failed to notch a win during the hard-court stretch leading up to New York.

Yet, Grand Slams seems to bring out his best, as he's always had a knack for raising his level on the biggest stages.

Given Zverev's recent success at majors, it's no surprise he's considered the favorite here.

Still, at 30 years old, chances like these won't come often for Khachanov. If he can find his forehand early, he is more than capable of pulling off the upset.

That being said, Zverev is still expected to prevail.

Prediction: No. 1 Alexander Zverev def. Karen Khachanov in 4 sets

Friday night at Arthur Ashe Stadium will showcase a rare treat for American tennis fans: Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe squaring off in only the third all-American men's US Open semifinal of the 21st century.

Both players arrive riding a wave of confidence after statement wins. Tiafoe engineered a miraculous rally, clawing back from two sets down to stun Alex Michelsen and keep his title hopes alive.

Shelton delivered the upset of the tournament, outlasting defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set epic that concluded at 3:33 a.m., marking the latest finish in US Open history.

Shelton is peaking at exactly the right moment. His booming serve can crack 150 MPH, but what truly separates him is his ability to combine all-out aggression with stubborn resilience on defense.

Tiafoe, always a force during the North American hard-court season, is making his third trip to the US Open semifinals and is hungry for his first shot at a Grand Slam final.

Like Shelton, Tiafoe's game revolves around a powerful serve and a heavy forehand. Tiafoe must avoid another slow start, as Shelton has not let up throughout the entire tournament.

Considering Shelton's current surge, he should have enough to get through.

Regardless, fans can expect an exciting showdown that is sure to be a must-watch.

Prediction: No. 8 Ben Shelton def. No. 11 Frances Tiafoe in 4 sets

articles.body:
Aryna Sabalenka is "ready for the fight" as she eyes a third straight title at the US Open, where the woman standing in her way, Elena Rybakina, has already ended Sabalenka's reign at number one in the world.

The blockbuster final in Flushing Meadows is a repeat of the Australian Open final in January won by Rybakina, who avenged a 2023 loss to Sabalenka in the Melbourne title match.

Sabalenka leads their head to head 10-7, including victories over Rybakina on the way to titles in the prestigious WTA 1000 events in Indian Wells and Miami in March.

But the 28-year-old Belarusian's results had tailed off since then, with disappointing exits at Roland Garros and Wimbledon.

She has reemerged as a dominant force at Flushing Meadows, where she delivered a near-flawless display of power and precision to beat Jessica Pegula in straight sets to reach her fourth straight US Open final.

Rybakina fought back from a set down to beat 2023 champion Coco Gauff and reach her first US Open final.

By then the 27-year-old was assured of supplanting Sabalenka atop the rankings by virtue of reaching the semi-finals.

It's a satisfying accomplishment for a player whose preparations for the tournament were clouded by a heel injury that forced her out of the tournament in Cincinnati last month and had her wondering if she would be able to play at all.

In fact, the injury has not appeared to be an issue, and Sabalenka was bracing for another demanding encounter.

"She's a big server. She really improved over the years on the baseline game," Sabalenka said. "So it's going to be a physically and mentally tough match.

"But I'm ready for the fight. I'm ready to do everything to get the win."

Rybakina, whose self-contained demeanor makes her a perfect foil to the fiery Sabalenka, also stressed the mental demands of a matchup that leaves no margin for error.

"She's a very aggressive player. It's difficult to play with her, mentally, physically, because she has a big game, a big serve," Rybakina said.

"I will need to come with all the energy I will have, bring my best serve against Aryna and make the right decisions in the right moment, because most of the times it's a tight, tight score. This is where the decision makes a difference."

Sabalenka, who leads the head to head 10-7, is the first player in the Open era to reach eight straight hard court Grand Slam finals, but she has stumbled in several.

Before her loss to Rybakina in Melbourne this year she was upset by Madison Keys there in 2025 -- the American spoiling Sabalenka's bid for third straight Australian title.

As she now tries to join Chris Evert and Serena Williams as the only women to win three consecutive US Open titles, Sabalenka says she has learned to tune out the noise surrounding the three-peat bid.

"It sounds simple, but it's not really simple to do sometimes," the four-time Grand Slam champion said.

A victory for Rybakina, whose second Grand Slam title in Australia came four years after her maiden major at Wimbledon, would further cement her status at the summit -- and as chief rival to Sabalenka.

But Rybakina insists their fierce on-court rivalry isn't personal.

"It's an important match," she said, but added: "Since it's a final I feel like it doesn't matter who is on the other side. You just want to win and do your best.

"But also, I don't want to put too much pressure on myself," she added.

Both players say that lifting the trophy come Saturday is more important than the No.1 ranking.

Sabalenka admitted it felt "a little bit weird" to know she'll lose the top spot after a dominant two weeks in New York, but if the fortnight ends with a title, she said: "I don't care."
